claims.text: Classical non-indexical models of divine omniscience cannot account for divine agency that is both libertarian and morally responsible.
claims.quote: I argue that classical non-indexical models of divine omniscience are insufficient to account for divine agency conceived as both libertarian and morally responsible.

claims.text: If an agent is robustly responsible for bringing about φ rather than ψ, the agent’s cognitive state must represent φ as the outcome of its own action rather than ψ.
claims.quote: (BP) Bridge Principle  If an agent is robustly responsible for bringing about φ rather than ψ, then the agent’s cognitive state must represent φ as the outcome of its own action rather than ψ.

claims.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires explanations that identify the agent as the source of one outcome rather than relevant alternatives.
claims.quote: (1) Robust contrastive responsibility requires explanations that fix the agent as the source of one outcome rather than relevant alternatives.

claims.text: Rationalising explanations that fix an agent as the responsible source of an outcome need irreducibly de se content, because third‑personal identification alone is insufficient.
claims.quote: (2) Rationalising explanations that fix an agent as the responsible source of an outcome require self-ascriptive, irreducibly de se content, because source-attribution is not exhausted by third-personal identification.

claims.text: Strong non‑indexical models of omniscience exclude irreducibly de se content.
claims.quote: (3) Strong non-indexical models of omniscience exclude irreducibly de se content.

claims.text: Therefore, strong non‑indexical models of omniscience cannot account for robust contrastive divine responsibility.
claims.quote: (4) Therefore, strong non-indexical models of omniscience cannot account for robust contrastive divine responsibility.

claims.text: If God is robustly responsible for actualising one world rather than another, divine cognition must include self‑locating content that represents God as the source of that actualisation.
claims.quote: The Self-Location Constraint (SLC) applies BP to the divine case. If God is robustly responsible for actualising one world rather than another, then divine cognition must include self-locating content representing God as the source of that actualisation.

claims.text: A third‑personal proposition such as ‘God actualises W1’ does not represent the actualisation as issued from God’s own activity, failing the requirement of robust responsibility.
claims.quote: A third-personal proposition such as “God actualises W1” may identify the correct agent extensionally, yet it does not by itself represent the actualisation under the first-personal aspect required for source attribution.

claims.text: De se cognition is constitutive of robust contrastive agency attribution, not merely an instrumental aid.
claims.quote: Rather, de se cognition is constitutive of robust contrastive agency attribution itself.

claims.text: Defenders of divine simplicity may argue that self‑locating content can be incorporated into a single timeless act of cognition without invoking metaphysical composition.
claims.quote: Defenders of divine simplicity may therefore resist the argument by showing how self-locating content can be included within a single simple act of cognition without metaphysical composition.

claims.text: The argument is conditional; those who reject libertarian agency or robust contrastive responsibility may reject premise (1).
claims.quote: The argument is conditional. Those who reject libertarian agency or robust contrastive responsibility may reject premise (1).

claims.text: Finite Perry‑style cases are illustrative, showing that the structural feature of agency explanation is not limited to cognitively constrained agents.
claims.quote: The appeal to finite cases is therefore illustrative rather than evidential. Perry-style cases illuminate a structural feature of agency explanation that, if genuine, is not confined to cognitively limited agents.

claims.text: The Self‑Location Constraint applies to any necessarily unique agent with libertarian powers and exclusively non‑indexical cognition.
claims.quote: Although developed within a theistic framework, the structure of SLC generalises to any necessarily unique agent with libertarian powers and exclusively non-indexical cognition.

claims.text: A strong non-indexical interpretation of omniscience claims that divine cognition contains no irreducible de se structure.
claims.quote: The target of the present argument is a strong non-indexical interpretation of omniscience: not merely the claim that divine knowledge is grounded in the divine essence, but the stronger claim that divine cognition contains no irreducible de se structure whatsoever.

claims.text: Divine cognition is identical with the divine essence, so God does not know God as a subject apprehending an object.
claims.quote: God therefore does not know God as a subject apprehending an independently given object, nor does divine cognition proceed through discursive inference or propositional mediation. Rather, the act of divine knowing is identical with the divine essence itself.

claims.text: Divine simplicity entails that God lacks any metaphysical composition, including distinctions between essence and existence.
claims.quote: God is taken to be free of all metaphysical composition, including distinctions between essence and existence, act and potency, substance and attribute.

claims.text: On stronger formulations of simplicity, divine omniscience, omnipotence, goodness, and being are numerically identical with the divine essence.
claims.quote: On stronger formulations of simplicity, divine omniscience, omnipotence, goodness, and being are all numerically identical with the divine essence.

claims.text: If the act, object, and subject of divine knowledge are identical, divine self‑knowledge contains no irreducibly first‑personal or self‑locating structure.
claims.quote: Since the act, object, and subject of divine knowledge are identical, divine self‑knowledge contains no irreducibly first‑personal or self‑locating structure.

claims.text: A defender of simplicity may argue that self‑locating content can be included within a single simple act of cognition without metaphysical composition.
claims.quote: A defender of simplicity may therefore resist the argument by showing how self‑locating content can be included within a single simple act of cognition without metaphysical composition.

claims.text: Thomistic defenders may appeal to analogical predication or the doctrine of the eternal divine act to resist modal differentiation within divine cognition.
claims.quote: Thomistic defenders of non‑indexical omniscience may appeal to analogical predication or to the doctrine of the eternal divine act in order to resist modal differentiation within divine cognition.

claims.text: A strictly non‑indexical conception of divine cognition cannot account for divine responsibility for actualising one world rather than another.
claims.quote: The difficulty, however, is that if God is robustly responsible for actualising one world rather than another, then divine cognition appears to require self‑locating content identifying God as the source of that actualisation.

claims.text: Consequently, divine omniscience cannot remain strictly non‑indexical if it must support libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility.
claims.quote: The remainder of the paper argues that, given libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility, it is not.

claims.text: The argument assumes that no adequately developed account currently exists that realizes irreducible de se content within a single timeless simple act of cognition.
claims.quote: The present claim is only that no adequately developed account of this kind is presently available.

claims.text: Can a single timeless and simple act of cognition realize irreducible de se content without violating divine simplicity?
claims.quote: A defender of classical theism may still argue that irreducible de se content can be realised within a single timeless and simple act of cognition without introducing metaphysical composition.

claims.text: Classical theism holds that divine omniscience is exhaustive but strictly non‑indexical, opposing the claim that self‑locating content is required.
claims.quote: Classical theism traditionally resists this conclusion. Divine omniscience is typically understood as timeless, non‑discursive, and complete without standpoint‑dependent representation.

claims.text: Purely uncentred knowledge is not sufficient for agency‑sensitive explanation given libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility.
claims.quote: The issue is not merely whether God knows all truths, but whether purely uncentred knowledge is sufficient for agency-sensitive explanation. The remainder of the paper argues that, given libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility, it is not.

claims.text: Knowing “God actualises W1” and that I = God preserves extensional truth but fails to determine the self‑ascriptive content needed for responsibility.
claims.quote: Knowledge that “God actualises W1”, together with the identity “I = God”, preserves extensional truth but does not by itself determine the self-ascriptive content involved in responsibility for actualising W1 rather than W0.

claims.text: Action explanation depends on which centre realises a true proposition, so third‑person truths underdetermine the de se content required for robust contrastive responsibility.
claims.quote: On centred-worlds semantics, action explanation is sensitive not merely to which proposition is true, but to which centre realises it. Third-personal truths therefore underdetermine the de se content required for robust contrastive responsibility.

claims.text: Substituting co‑referring expressions preserves truth but not explanatory role; knowing God actualises W1 is not equivalent to representing oneself as the source of that actualisation.
claims.quote: Substitution of co-referring expressions preserves extensional truth but need not preserve explanatory role. Knowing that God actualises W1 is not equivalent, in action-guiding contexts, to representing oneself as the source of actualising W1 rather than W0.

claims.text: If robust contrastive responsibility demands explanation of why an outcome is attributable to the agent rather than alternatives, then de se content is indispensable.
claims.quote: If robust contrastive responsibility requires explanation of why this outcome is attributable to this agent rather than relevant alternatives, then de se content appears indispensable.

claims.text: Even timeless divine knowledge must distinguish the actualised world from merely possible worlds, requiring cognition to account for W1 as actualised through divine agency.
claims.quote: Even on timeless models of divine knowledge, actualisation introduces an explanatory asymmetry between W1 and relevant alternatives. Divine cognition must therefore account for W1 as actualised through divine agency rather than merely possible.

claims.text: Strong non‑indexical omniscience faces the difficulty of explaining the explanatory asymmetry between actualised and possible worlds without irreducible self‑locating content.
claims.quote: The difficulty for strong non-indexicality is explaining how such asymmetry can be accounted for without irreducibly self-locating content.

claims.text: The Self‑Location Constraint requires a cognitive state to represent both which outcome obtains and the subject as the source of that outcome.
claims.quote: A cognitive state satisfies SLC only if it represents both which outcome obtains and the subject as the source of that outcome.

claims.text: Non‑indexical omniscience, understood as exhaustive knowledge of all true uncentred propositions, is insufficient for explaining libertarian and contrastively responsible divine agency.
claims.quote: The central claim is that non-indexical omniscience, understood as exhaustive knowledge of all true uncentred propositions, is insufficient for explaining libertarian and contrastively responsible divine agency.

claims.text: “God actualises W1 rather than W0” plus I = God yields the same uncentred truth conditions as “I actualise W1 rather than W0”, but the latter includes self‑locating content the former lacks.
claims.quote: Knowledge that “God actualises W1 rather than W0”, together with the identity “I = God”, may determine the same uncentred truth conditions as “I actualise W1 rather than W0”. Yet the latter contains self-locating content absent from the former.

claims.text: Substituting co‑referring expressions may preserve truth while changing explanatory role; an agent can know all third‑person facts about an action yet lack cognition that represents the action as issued from its own agency.
claims.quote: Substitution of co-referring expressions may preserve truth while altering explanatory role. An agent may know every relevant third-personal fact concerning an action while lacking the cognition required to represent that action as issuing from its own agency.

claims.text: If there are no genuine modal alternatives—e.g., God necessarily actualises W1—then the contrastive explanatory demand does not arise.
claims.quote: If there are no genuine modal alternatives—for example, if God necessarily actualises W1—then the contrastive explanatory demand does not arise.

claims.text: The argument relies on a robust contrastive conception of responsibility and libertarian divine agency, which may be objected to.
claims.quote: The argument developed thus far is conditional upon a robust contrastive conception of responsibility together with libertarian divine agency. Several objections may nevertheless be raised against the SLC and its implications for divine omniscience.

claims.text: The argument only targets a strictly non‑indexical view of omniscience; defenders of classical theism could preserve simplicity while including de se representation, so incompatibility is not established.
claims.quote: The present argument therefore targets only a stronger claim: that divine omniscience is wholly non-indexical and contains no irreducible self-locating content. If a defender of simplicity can explain how divine cognition includes the de se representation required for contrastive responsibility while preserving metaphysical simplicity, then the argument does not establish the incompatibility of simplicity and omniscience.

claims.text: Classical theism affirms maximal cognition, simplicity, and morally significant agency.
claims.quote: The divine case sharpens this tension because classical theism simultaneously affirms maximal cognition, simplicity, and morally significant agency.

claims.text: An objection denies that irreducible de se content is required for divine agency explanation.
claims.quote: The most direct objection denies that irreducible de se content is explanatorily required in the divine case.

claims.text: The objection conflates extensional equivalence with explanatory equivalence.
claims.quote: This objection, however, conflates extensional equivalence with explanatory equivalence.

claims.text: Self‑locating cognition performs an explanatory role not exhausted by third‑personal representation.
claims.quote: The central claim of the de se literature is not merely that indexical expressions behave differently in language, but that self‑locating cognition performs an explanatory role not exhausted by third‑personal representation.

claims.text: Knowing that God actualises W1 rather than W0 does not represent divine agency for contrastive explanation.
claims.quote: Knowledge that “God actualises W1 rather than W0” specifies which contrastive outcome obtains, but does not yet represent divine agency under the aspect required for contrastive explanation.

claims.text: Robust contrastive responsibility requires cognition that explains why an outcome is attributable to a specific agent rather than alternatives.
claims.quote: Robust contrastive responsibility requires more than accurate description of an outcome. It requires cognition capable of explaining why this outcome is attributable to this agent rather than relevant alternatives.

claims.text: An objection claims that God knows the actual world because God causes it.
claims.quote: A related objection appeals to divine knowledge-by-causation. God knows the actual world because God causes it.

claims.text: The reductionist strategy only shows extensional equivalence and fails to meet the explanatory demands of robust contrastive responsibility.
claims.quote: The reductionist strategy therefore establishes, at most, extensional equivalence. It does not show that exhaustive third‑personal cognition is sufficient for the explanatory demands imposed by robust contrastive responsibility.

claims.text: A sophisticated response asserts that divine cognition can include de se structure without introducing metaphysical composition.
claims.quote: A more sophisticated response grants that divine cognition must include de se structure while denying that this introduces metaphysical composition into the divine nature.

claims.text: The question is whether irreducible de se representation can be an intensional feature of a single simple act rather than an added ontological component.
claims.quote: The relevant question is therefore whether irreducible de se representation can be understood as an intensional feature of a single simple act rather than as an additional ontological component.

claims.text: A radical response rejects the assumptions that generate the SLC.
claims.quote: A more radical response rejects the assumptions generating the SLC altogether.

claims.text: If God could not have acted otherwise, there is no contrastive question about why W1 rather than W0, eliminating the need for self‑locating representation.
claims.quote: If God could not have actualised otherwise, then there is no contrastive question concerning why W1 obtains rather than W0. The need for self‑locating representation across alternatives correspondingly disappears.

claims.text: Strong non‑indexical omniscience is insufficient for explaining libertarian and contrastively responsible divine agency.
claims.quote: This paper has argued that strong non‑indexical conceptions of omniscience are insufficient for explaining libertarian and contrastively responsible divine agency.

claims.text: Classical theism faces explanatory tension among robust libertarian agency, wholly non‑indexical omniscience, and simplicity that excludes irreducible de se structure.
claims.quote: The argument therefore suggests that classical theism faces explanatory tension among three commitments when each is maintained in its strongest form: robust libertarian agency, wholly non‑indexical omniscience, and divine simplicity interpreted as excluding irreducible de se structure.

claims.text: Worship-worthiness should be treated as the foundational question of philosophy of religion.
claims.quote: This paper argues that worship-worthiness should be treated as the foundational question of philosophy of religion.

claims.text: The philosophy of worship can be divided into two branches: the axiology of worship and the deontology of worship.
claims.quote: I divide the philosophy of worship into two branches: the axiology of worship (whether God is worthy of worship) and the deontology of worship (whether we ought to worship God).

claims.text: Worship‑Worthiness Theology has axiological, prudential, and methodological priority over Non‑Worship‑Worthiness Theology, which is the “Worship‑Worthiness First” thesis.
claims.quote: I argue that WWT has axiological, prudential, and methodological priority over NWWT – a thesis I call Worship-Worthiness First.

claims.text: Because worship is central to religious life, questions of worship‑worthiness cannot remain philosophically secondary.
claims.quote: If worship is central to religious life, then questions of worship‑worthiness cannot remain philosophically secondary.

claims.text: A being may be worthy of worship even if we are not obligated to worship it, and we may be obligated to worship something unworthy of worship.
claims.quote: A being might be worthy of worship even if we are not obligated to worship it, and we might be obligated to worship something unworthy of worship.

claims.text: A being is worthy of worship only when there are right‑kind reasons to worship it.
claims.quote: A being is worthy of worship only when there are right kind of reasons to worship it.

claims.text: The axiology of worship concerns questions of fittingness and worship‑worthiness.
claims.quote: The axiology of worship concerns questions of fittingness and worship‑worthiness, including the following:

claims.text: The deontology of worship concerns normative questions such as obligation, reasonableness, and justification of worship.
claims.quote: The deontology of worship concerns normative questions about worship, including the following:

claims.text: Despite its religious significance, worship has not received sustained philosophical attention.
claims.quote: Yet despite its religious significance, worship has not received sustained philosophical attention.

claims.text: Worship is a central feature of many religious traditions.
claims.quote: Worship is a central feature of many religious traditions.

claims.text: Hazony Levi claims that many philosophers are mistaken in treating worship as a unified concept with a single essence across times and places.
claims.quote: she claims that many philosophers have been mistaken in treating worship as a unified concept with a single essence shared across times and places.

claims.text: Although worship shows historical diversity, this does not demonstrate that worship is philosophically indefinable.
claims.quote: Hazony Levi is right to emphasize the historical diversity of worship, but this does not show that worship is philosophically indefinable.

claims.text: The question “What is worship?” is a metatheological question that depends on broader conceptions of God, the self, and their relation.
claims.quote: The question ‘What is worship?’ is not a purely descriptive or historical question. It is what I call a metatheological question – one that depends on broader conceptions of God, the self, and the relation between them.

claims.text: Worship‑worthiness is not merely one topic among others; it should guide and structure all other philosophical questions about God.
claims.quote: Worship‑worthiness, this paper argues, is not one topic among others. It is the question that should guide and structure all the others.

claims.text: There is no fully neutral or tradition‑independent answer to the question of worship.
claims.quote: There is no fully neutral or tradition-independent answer to the question of worship.

claims.text: Definitions of worship are not simply discovered but are adopted in light of broader theological and philosophical commitments.
claims.quote: It means that definitions of worship are not simply discovered, but adopted in light of broader theological and philosophical commitments.

claims.text: Philosophers of worship should proceed like philosophers of faith, drawing on diverse traditions while still offering their own philosophical definitions.
claims.quote: Thus, philosophers of worship should proceed in much the same way that philosophers of faith do: they may draw on the diverse ways religious traditions understand worship while still offering philosophical definitions of their own.

claims.text: Neither attitude‑based nor action‑based accounts of worship is adequate on its own.
claims.quote: Neither approach, I argue, is adequate on its own.

claims.text: Some degree of action is necessary for worship.
claims.quote: Thus, some degree of action is necessary for worship.

claims.text: Action without the appropriate inner state falls short of genuine worship.
claims.quote: Action without the appropriate inner state falls short of genuine worship.

claims.text: The cognitive and affective components are more fundamental to worship than the practical component.
claims.quote: These two cases suggest an important conclusion: the cognitive and affective components are more fundamental to worship, while the practical component plays a primarily expressive role.

claims.text: A tripartite account of worship requires relevant beliefs, appropriate emotions, and a disposition to perform expressive actions.
claims.quote: For A to worship B requires that: (1) A has relevant beliefs about B, (2) A has appropriate emotions toward B, and (3) A is disposed to perform actions that express or reinforce those beliefs and emotions.

claims.text: The tripartite account belongs to attitude‑based accounts but refines them by separating cognitive and affective components and assigning action an expressive role.
claims.quote: This account belongs broadly within the family of attitude-based accounts, though with two important refinements.

claims.text: Normative questions about belief, emotion, and action must be answered before determining what kind of being could be worship‑worthy.
claims.quote: These are normative questions that any full philosophy of worship must address before determining what kind of being, if any, could be worthy of worship.

claims.text: James Rachels argues that worship entails unconditional submission, which is incompatible with moral autonomy, so no being can be worthy of worship.
claims.quote: James Rachels famously argued that worship entails unconditional submission, and since such submission is incompatible with moral autonomy, no being can be worthy of worship.

claims.text: Occasional disobedience caused by weakness of will may not be sufficient to exclude a person from worship.
claims.quote: Occasional disobedience resulting from weakness of will, for example, may not suffice for exclusion from worship.

claims.text: Worship‑Worthiness First (WWF) holds that worship‑worthiness‑first approaches have priority over non‑worship‑worthiness‑first approaches.
claims.quote: Worship‑Worthiness First (WWF): WWT has priority over NWWT.

claims.text: Before asking whether God exists or what properties God possesses, we must first ask what is worthy of worship.
claims.quote: Before asking whether God exists or what properties God possesses, we must first ask what is worthy of worship – and that question cannot be answered without addressing the normative questions raised here.

claims.text: Worship‑Worthiness First (WWF) holds that worship‑worthiness theory (WWT) has priority over non‑worship‑worthiness theory (NWWT).
claims.quote: Worship-Worthiness First (WWF): WWT has priority over NWWT.

claims.text: One possible interpretation of WWF is logical priority, the view that the term ‘God’ simply means ‘worthy of worship’.
claims.quote: One possible interpretation of WWF is logical priority: the view that ‘God’ simply means ‘worthy of worship’.

claims.text: The author does not accept the logical‑priority view that defines God as worthy of worship.
claims.quote: I do not take this view.

claims.text: Descriptively, the term ‘God’ is used in many ways that are independent of worship‑worthiness.
claims.quote: As a descriptive matter, the term ‘God’ is used in many ways that are independent of worship‑worthiness.

claims.text: The possibility of misotheism shows one can coherently affirm God’s existence while denying that God is worthy of worship.
claims.quote: the possibility of misotheism – the view that God exists but is worthy of hatred rather than love or worship – shows that one may coherently affirm God’s existence while denying that God is worthy of worship.

claims.text: Worship‑worthiness theory (WWT) has priority over NWWT in several respects.
claims.quote: Yet it has priority over NWWT in several respects.

claims.text: A worship‑worthy God transforms the value of human life in a way that a purely metaphysical first cause may not.
claims.quote: A worship‑worthy God transforms the value of human life in a way that a purely metaphysical first cause may not.

claims.text: Worship engages believers cognitively, affectively, and practically, reorienting their life, shaping values, and giving them an ideal to aspire to.
claims.quote: Worship engages the believer cognitively, affectively, and practically. It reorients their life, shapes their values, and gives them an ideal to aspire to.

claims.text: From an axiological standpoint, a worship‑worthy God is especially significant because its existence profoundly affects human life’s value and orientation.
claims.quote: Thus, from the standpoint of the axiology of theism, the God of WWT is especially significant, since the existence of a worship‑worthy God would make a profound difference to the value and orientation of human life.

claims.text: Our intellectual and practical resources are finite, so we cannot pursue every philosophical question with equal urgency.
claims.quote: Because our intellectual and practical resources are finite, we cannot pursue every question with equal urgency.

claims.text: Prudentially, because WWT makes a greater axiological difference, we should focus on WWT before other questions.
claims.quote: If, as I have argued, the God of WWT makes a greater axiological difference than the kinds of God typically emphasized within NWWT, then prudentially – given the finitude of our time – we should focus on WWT first.

claims.text: Methodologically, we should adopt WWT as the starting point, asking what is worthy of worship before any other theological question.
claims.quote: If we accept both the axiological priority and the prudential priority of WWT, then a further consequence follows: we should also adopt WWT as our methodological starting point.

claims.text: Perfect Being Thesis: God is the being than which no greater is metaphysically possible.
claims.quote: Perfect Being Thesis: God is the being than which no greater is metaphysically possible.

claims.text: Worship‑Worthiness Reading of Perfect Being Theism: God is the being than which no more worship‑worthy being can be conceived.
claims.quote: Worship‑Worthiness Reading of Perfect Being Theism: God is the being than which no more worship‑worthy being can be conceived.

claims.text: God need not be omnipotent in every detail; it may suffice that he is powerful enough to create the universe.
claims.quote: We may not need to insist that God is omnipotent in every detail; it may be enough that he is powerful enough to create the universe (Gale and Pruss 1999, 468, 473).

claims.text: God need not be omnibenevolent; it may suffice that he is vastly superior to us in goodness.
claims.quote: We may not need to insist on omnibenevolence; it may be enough that he is vastly superior to us in goodness.

claims.text: It would be absurd to say that a being becomes worthy of worship only after learning a trivial fact.
claims.quote: It would be absurd to say that such a being becomes worthy of worship only after learning that trivial fact.

claims.text: Worship‑worthiness may not require the full Omni‑God Thesis.
claims.quote: This suggests that worship‑worthiness may not require the full Omni‑God Thesis.

claims.text: Ninian Smart rejected the premise that necessary existence is required for worship‑worthiness.
claims.quote: Ninian Smart responded by rejecting premise (2): necessary existence is not required for worship‑worthiness (Smart 1972, 55–59).

claims.text: Metaphysical questions are being approached through the lens of worship‑worthiness rather than the other way around.
claims.quote: The crucial point is that metaphysical questions are here being approached through the lens of worship‑worthiness rather than the other way around.

claims.text: WWF claims that questions about divine attributes should be guided by worship‑worthiness rather than settled independently of it.
claims.quote: This case illustrates the broader methodological claim of WWF: questions about divine attributes should be guided by worship‑worthiness rather than settled independently of it.

claims.text: WWF views the standard treatment of arguments for God’s existence as methodologically backwards.
claims.quote: From the perspective of WWF, however, the standard treatment of these arguments is methodologically backwards.

claims.text: A sound argument that proves a ‘ferocious beast’ God would not lead us to worship such a being.
claims.quote: Suppose a sound argument proved that God exists – but the God it proves is the ‘ferocious beast’ described by al‑Ghazālī at the beginning of this paper: a being who does not care about destroying the world, who is never affected, and before whom we should stand in fear.

claims.text: Even if the argument from disorder is sound, it gives no reason to worship the being it proves.
claims.quote: Suppose this argument is sound. Does it give us any reason to worship the being it proves?

claims.text: Gale and Pruss argue that having enough power to create the universe suffices for God to be a fitting object of worship.
claims.quote: Gale and Pruss suggest that omnipotence is not required for worship‑worthiness. What matters is that God has enough power to create the universe – and that, they claimed, is enough for God to be a fitting object of worship (Gale and Pruss 1999, 468, 473).

claims.text: If worship requires address and address requires a hearer who can understand, then the object of worship must be a personal being.
claims.quote: If worship requires address, and address requires a hearer capable of understanding, then the object of worship must be a person – a being with a mind and will.

claims.text: Does worship‑worthiness require that God be moral?
claims.quote: The primary question is: ‘Does worship‑worthiness require that God be moral?’

claims.text: Lewis assumes that worship-worthiness is ultimately grounded in moral worthiness.
claims.quote: Lewis assumes that worship-worthiness is ultimately grounded in moral worthiness.

claims.text: Lewis's assumption that worship-worthiness is grounded in moral worthiness is not obviously true.
claims.quote: But this assumption is not obviously true.

claims.text: One can take worship-worthiness seriously without taking morality as the ultimate standard.
claims.quote: The examples we have seen – from earlier societies that worshipped God primarily as sovereign power to Mulgan’s recent defence of a non-benevolent God – suggest that one can take worship-worthiness seriously without taking morality as the ultimate standard.

claims.text: Whether morality is required for worship-worthiness should be decided within the axiology of worship, not presupposed independently.
claims.quote: If anything, the explanatory order runs in the opposite direction: whether morality is required for worship-worthiness is a question to be settled within the axiology of worship, rather than presupposed independently of it.

claims.text: Before asking whether God exists or what properties God has, we should first ask what kind of being is worthy of worship.
claims.quote: This paper has defended a central claim: before asking whether God exists or what properties God has, we should first ask what kind of being is worthy of worship.

claims.text: The philosophy of worship splits into the axiology of worship (whether God is worthy) and the deontology of worship (whether we ought to worship God).
claims.quote: I first distinguished two branches of the philosophy of worship: the axiology of worship (whether God is worthy of worship) and the deontology of worship (whether we ought to worship God).

claims.text: Worship‑Worthiness Theology (WWT) has priority over Non‑Worship‑Worthiness Theology (NWWT).
claims.quote: My claim is that WWT has priority over NWWT.

claims.text: The priority of WWT is axiological, prudential, and methodological.
claims.quote: This priority is not logical (I do not define ‘God’ as ‘worthy of worship’). Rather, it is axiological (the God of WWT makes the greatest difference to the value of human life), prudential (given our limited resources, we should focus on what matters most), and methodological (the order of inquiry must begin with worship-worthiness).

claims.text: Starting from worship‑worthiness rather than metaphysical perfection may allow us to dispense with strong forms of omnipotence, omniscience, and omnibenevolence.
claims.quote: In perfect being theism, starting from worship-worthiness rather than metaphysical perfection may yield a lighter set of commitments: we may not need omnipotence, omniscience, or omnibenevolence in their strongest forms.

claims.text: An argument that proves only a first cause or necessary being, without addressing worship‑worthiness, misses the point entirely.
claims.quote: In arguments for God’s existence, worship-worthiness changes the standard of evaluation: an argument that proves only a first cause or a necessary being, without addressing whether such a being is worthy of worship, misses the point entirely.

claims.text: The key issue is whether personhood or moral goodness is required for worship‑worthiness, not simply whether God is personal or morally good.
claims.quote: The fundamental issue is not simply whether God is personal or morally good, but whether personhood or moral goodness is required for worship-worthiness in the first place.

claims.text: If worship requires minimal cognitive grasp and love, a wholly unknowable God may be impossible to love, pressuring apophatic conceptions.
claims.quote: If worship requires some minimal cognitive grasp of its object – and if, as I have argued, love and awe are constitutive elements of worship – then a God who is wholly unknowable may become difficult or even impossible to love.

claims.text: The claim that WWT has axiological, prudential, and methodological priority over rival approaches is new.
claims.quote: What is new in this paper is the claim that WWT has such priority, and that this priority should significantly reorient central debates within philosophy of religion.

claims.text: Process theology limits divine power in response to the problem of evil.
claims.quote: process theology, which limits divine power in response to the problem of evil.

claims.text: Omnipotence is less important for worship-worthiness than attributes such as knowledge and benevolence.
claims.quote: Audi suggests that omnipotence is less important for worship-worthiness than attributes such as knowledge and benevolence (Audi 2011, 237–238).

claims.text: Divine simplicity is the claim that God is not a composite of more basic features.
claims.quote: the notion of divine simplicity, the idea that God is not a composite of more basic features

claims.text: Traditional theists hold that God’s nature is absolutely simple, identical with God, so any dependence on the nature is merely self‑dependence.
claims.quote: God does have a nature, but that nature is absolutely simple – the property of being God, if you will – and so, the divine nature is not a composite of disparate properties out of God’s control. Moreover, God is identical with that nature, and so while God is dependent upon his nature, the dependence is an innocuous case of self‑dependence.

claims.text: Divine simplicity conflicts with the fact that God possesses several properties such as knowledge, power, and will.
claims.quote: divine simplicity flies in the face of the fact that God has several properties, such as knowledge, power, will

claims.text: If God is identical with a single property, then God is a property rather than a person, which is absurd.
claims.quote: if God is identical with that property, God is a property, not a person, which seems absurd

claims.text: Al‑Ghazālī’s critique of divine simplicity anticipates and exceeds Plantinga’s own criticism.
claims.quote: the renowned Muslim theologian Abū Ḥāmid al‑Ghazālī (d. 1111) subjects the philosophical doctrine of simplicity and the grounds for accepting it to a scathing critique, which interestingly anticipates and goes beyond Plantinga’s own critique

claims.text: Avicenna’s stronger version of divine simplicity can answer some of Plantinga’s objections.
claims.quote: Avicenna’s stronger version of divine simplicity can respond to some of Plantinga’s objections

claims.text: Avicenna assumes that if God had distinct properties, those properties would be parts of a whole.
claims.quote: the first assumption is that if God were to have distinct properties, these properties would stand to God as parts to a whole

claims.text: Avicenna assumes that parts taken individually differ from the whole taken collectively.
claims.quote: Avicenna’s second mereological assumption is that parts (or at least proper parts) taken individually are other than or different from the whole taken collectively

claims.text: It is contradictory for something to exist both through itself and through another.
claims.quote: It is simply a contradiction for something to exist both through itself and through another; it is tantamount to saying that something’s existence depends on nothing and depends on something

claims.text: Therefore, the Necessary Existent (God) cannot be a composite; consequently, God’s existence is simple.
claims.quote: Therefore, the Necessary Existent through itself, that is, God, cannot be a composite and if he is not a composite yet he exists, God’s existence is simple

claims.text: Traditional theists fear that a composite God would be causally dependent on his distinct properties.
claims.quote: for traditional theists it is fundamentally the fear that a composite God, that is, a God having distinct properties, attributes, or the like, is in some way causally dependent upon those properties

claims.text: If God were not simple, he would depend on properties like power, wisdom, and blessedness as final causes.
claims.quote: if God were not simple, he would depend upon properties like power, wisdom, blessedness, in the order of final causation

claims.text: Plantinga argues that God possesses accidental properties that correspond to Avicennan relational properties.
claims.quote: Plantinga begins by first arguing that God has accidental properties, which seem to correspond to Avicennan relational properties.

claims.text: Avicenna holds that relational properties do not threaten divine simplicity, while Plantinga maintains that they do.
claims.quote: Avicenna believes that relational properties do not threaten divine simplicity, whereas Plantinga thinks that they do.

claims.text: Avicenna claims relational properties are not genuine properties in the sense of constitutive features.
claims.quote: For Avicenna, purportedly relational properties are not really properties at all, at least not in the sense of constitutive features.

claims.text: Plantinga asserts that possessing a given characterization makes God different from what He would have been without it.
claims.quote: Moreover, maintains Plantinga, possessing a given characterization does make God ‘different from what he would have been had it not characterized him’.

claims.text: Medieval philosophers agree that God’s many actions can be traced to Him, but these effects need not arise from distinct essential properties or characterizations.
claims.quote: Both sides in the medieval debate agreed that God’s ultimately numerous different actions or effects can be traced back to God; however, they also insisted that those different effects of his action need not emanate from different essential properties or even necessarily from different ways of characterizing God.

claims.text: The shift from properties to characteristics does not indicate real differences within the divinity.
claims.quote: Thus, Plantinga’s shift from properties to characteristics need not show that there are real differences within the divinity.

claims.text: Avicenna argues that God’s knowledge of a thing is the ultimate cause of that thing’s existence, so knowing and creating are identical in God.
claims.quote: Avicenna anticipates Plantinga’s own examples of creating and knowing, and explicitly argues that God’s knowledge of a thing is the ultimate cause of that thing’s existence. In other words, according to Avicenna for God to know the world, which includes Adam, is for God to create the world, which includes Adam.

claims.text: According to the traditional view, God lacks all potentiality and is fully actual, unlike humans whose knowing is a potentiality.
claims.quote: In the case of humans, knowing is a type of potentiality we have, whereas on the traditional view of God, God is devoid of all potentiality and instead God is fully actual.

claims.text: Plantinga challenges the claim that God has no potential properties, asserting that God later acquires such properties.
claims.quote: He challenges the claim that God has no potential properties, which he subsequently acquires.

claims.text: Plantinga’s intuition is that it seems right to think God lacks characteristics he could have had but may acquire.
claims.quote: The reason he gives for holding his preferred position is ‘it seems right to think that there are characteristics [God] lacks but could have had. It is natural to think, furthermore, that among these there are some he hasn’t yet acquired but could acquire’ (Plantinga (1980), 44).

claims.text: Plantinga defines a potential property as one that God lacks at some time t1 and possesses at a later time t2.
claims.quote: Given Plantinga’s subsequent challenge to the traditionalists’ assumption about God’s relation to time, at least in Does God Have a Nature, he seems to understand ‘potential property’ in terms of temporal frequency: x has some potential property, P, just in case there is a time t1 when x does not possess P, and then some subsequent time t2 when x does possess P.

claims.text: Ghazali maintains that all of God’s relational properties involve volition, which requires choosing among possible options.
claims.quote: Ghazālī insists that all of God’s relational properties involve God’s volition, and that volition must involve choosing among different possible options.

claims.text: Ghazali and other theologians object that Avicenna’s notion of volition makes God compelled and not truly sovereign.
claims.quote: It certainly did for Ghazālī and other theologians, who thought it so eviscerated the notion of will as to make God compelled, even if by his nature, and so not truly sovereign.

claims.text: The view Ghazali opposes holds that if God were not simple, He would be causally dependent on parts, threatening His aseity.
claims.quote: God purportedly must be simple, otherwise he is causally dependent upon his parts by way of material causality, and so his aseity is challenged.

claims.text: Ghazālī recasts God’s relation to attributes as a self and its attributes rather than as a whole constituted by parts.
claims.quote: First, he recasts the description of God’s relation to his attributes or properties in terms of a self and attributes that characterize that self rather than in terms of a whole constituted by its parts.

claims.text: Ghazālī questions whether the Aristotelian notion of material causation is a genuine form of causation or merely a technical term.
claims.quote: Second, he questions whether the Aristotelian notion of material causation is a genuine form of causation or just a term of art.

claims.text: Ghazālī advises abandoning the description of God as the Necessary Existent through itself, emphasizing instead that God is the eternally uncaused cause of everything.
claims.quote: Third, he counsels doing away with describing God as the Necessary Existent through itself, since the most important description is that the divine is the eternally uncaused cause of everything else.

claims.text: The relation between the divine self and its attributes is a grounding relation, not a causal relation.
claims.quote: In effect, as we shall see, Ghazālī suggests that the relation between the divine self and its attributes is a grounding relation rather than a causal relation.

claims.text: An efficient cause requires the cause to be extrinsic to its effect and the effect to derive its existence from the cause; the divine self and attributes are not extrinsic, so no efficient cause exists.
claims.quote: Here presumably Ghazālī intends Avicenna’s own account of an efficient cause: x is an efficient cause of y just in case (1) x is extrinsic to y and (2) y has its existence from x.

claims.text: If God needs anything for his existence or perfection, then he is not absolutely self‑sufficient, jeopardizing his aseity.
claims.quote: Thus, one might object that given that God is the Necessary Existent through itself, God cannot need anything for his existence and perfection. If God needs anything, then he is not absolutely self‑sufficient...

claims.text: If God is identical with each of his properties, then God has only one property, contradicting the fact that God possesses several distinct properties.
claims.quote: Plantinga identifies the ‘substantial’ difficulty as this: ‘If God is identical with each of his properties, then each of his properties is identical with each of his properties, so that God has but one property. This seems flatly incompatible with the obvious fact that God has several properties’.

claims.text: Ghazālī notes that different divine attributes have distinct accounts, meanings, or senses, so they are not all the same.
claims.quote: Such attributions as existing necessarily, knowing, willing, etc. all have different accounts, meanings, or senses (maʿānin) observes Ghazālī.

claims.text: Ghazālī fully agrees with this objection, confirming the problem.
claims.quote: Ghazālī wholly concurs.

claims.text: Asserting that God knows things other than himself entails abandoning divine simplicity.
claims.quote: If, conversely, one asserts that God knows things other than himself, as Avicenna did, then, claims Ghazālī, one implicitly has given up divine simplicity.

claims.text: The knowledge of oneself is distinct from the knowledge of another.
claims.quote: That is because the knowledge of oneself is distinct and different from the knowledge of another.

claims.text: Within God there are at least two distinct entities: his knowledge of himself and his knowledge of the world.
claims.quote: Consequently, within God there are at least two distinct things, namely, his knowledge of himself and additionally his knowledge of the other, that is, the world.

claims.text: Avicenna claimed that God’s knowledge of others is identical with his knowledge of himself.
claims.quote: Avicenna had attempted to avoid this conclusion by saying that God’s knowledge of others is identical with his knowledge of himself.

claims.text: Causation involves a relation (iḍāfa) between cause and effect.
claims.quote: Causation involves a relation (iḍāfa), namely, between the cause and the effect.

claims.text: If God knows that he is causing, then there must be multiplicity in divine knowledge.
claims.quote: Consequently, if God knows that he is causing – and recall that Avicenna’s own account of divine volition required that God does know that he is acting – and God’s causing is different from God, as Ghazālī believes he has shown, there must be multiplicity in the divine knowledge.

claims.text: Divine simplicity is incompatible with God’s omniscience.
claims.quote: In short, concludes Ghazālī, divine simplicity is incompatible with God’s omniscience.

claims.text: When forced to choose, omniscience is clearly required for God, while simplicity is not obviously required.
claims.quote: If one must decide between the two, the decision is obvious: anything worthy of the title God must be omniscient, whereas it is not at all obvious that it must be simple.

claims.text: The biconditional NEC‑G states that God necessarily exists if and only if in every possible world there exists a relevant counterpart of God.

claims.text: Because individuals are world‑bound and because of NEC‑G, God’s necessary existence depends on having a counterpart in every possible world, not on existing in all worlds.

claims.text: If God necessarily exists, there must be infinitely many world‑bound God‑counterparts, contradicting Anselmian Theism’s claim that there is only one unique God, thus threatening monotheism.

claims.text: Sheehy and Davis’s objection merely rejects counterpart theory as an adequate account of de re necessity, treating it as generally inadequate.

claims.text: Counterpart theory allows an ordinary individual like Bill to be possibly F because otherworldly Bill‑like counterparts are F, without threatening Bill’s uniqueness.
claims.quote: Indeed, if having, say, a Bill-counterpart in w is enough to make a de re possibility claim about Bill—and not the Bill-counterpart—true, then this apparatus should work for de re necessity claims of God; if only one Bill exists, yet Bill is possibly F because otherworldly-Billlike individuals are F, why should it be different for God’s necessary existence?

claims.text: In Anselmian Theism, a God‑like individual must be unique across all worlds, not merely within each world.

claims.quote: But this, I argue, comes at the cost of violating the uniqueness requirement: if we—so to speak—look down on logical space, we see a plurality of God-like individuals.

claims.quote: A well‑known objection to divine simplicity holds that the doctrine is incompatible with God's contingent knowledge.

claims.text: The author rejects two problematic solutions to this objection.
claims.quote: I set out the objection and reject two problematic solutions.

claims.text: The best answer is an extrinsic model of divine knowing, with no intrinsic change in God.
claims.quote: I then argue that the objection is best answered by adopting an "extrinsic model of divine knowing" according to which God's contingent knowledge, which varies across worlds, does not involve any intrinsic variation in God.

claims.text: The contingency objection threatens God's freedom.
claims.quote: The objection is taken to pose a threat to God's freedom.

claims.text: Tomaszewski argues the supporting argument for the contingency objection is invalid.
claims.quote: Tomaszewski argues that the argument that supports the contingency objection, however, is invalid.

claims.text: Two valid versions of the argument can be given, so the classical theist must defuse it.
claims.quote: I supply two valid versions of the argument; thus, the classical theist is required to defuse the argument.

claims.text: I assume God’s omnipotence is best understood as having all powers, meaning his power is wide‑ranging.
claims.quote: I’m going to assume that God’s omnipotence is best understood in terms of thinking about powers, and that we should understand ‘all’, which concerns the range of God’s power, as merely implying that God’s power is wide ranging.

claims.text: Torrance’s simplicity doctrine allows composites and historical contingencies, contrary to traditional simplicity.
claims.quote: Torrance’s doctrine of simplicity does not fully accord with the traditional one that does not allow for any form of introduction of composites and any historical contingencies into the Being of God.

claims.text: Torrance says God embraces created temporality and carnality in his eternal Being through Christ.
claims.quote: On Torrance’s account, God embraces created temporality and carnality into his eternal Being through Jesus Christ.

claims.text: Divine being is self‑determined in Trinitarian economic acts, making historical dissonance part of God’s simple disclosure.
claims.quote: Since the divine being is self‑determined in the economic acts of the Trinity, the moments of dissonance in the history of salvation become ineluctable components of God's simple, harmonious, and temporal disclosure of himself.

claims.text: Critics claim simplicity reduces God to an abstract property and makes theological language vacuous.
claims.quote: Critics of divine simplicity argue that simplicity leads us to identify God with an abstract property and that it renders theological language semantically vacuous because divine simplicity cannot ground a plurality of true intrinsic predicates.

claims.text: The Thomistic doctrine of analogy keeps theological language determinate without reintroducing composition in God.
claims.quote: I conclude by arguing that the Thomistic doctrine of analogy does not eliminate semantic openness but renders theological language sufficiently determinate for meaning and practice, grounding meaningful God‑talk in both metaphysics and the formative practices of religious life.

claims.text: The abstract raises two key problems: how a simple God can do and know many things, and whether a simple God could have acted otherwise.
claims.quote: Two key problems are: How can a simple God do and know many different things? And, could a simple God have done other than He has done?

claims.text: Anselm holds that a simple, eternal God can do and know a vast multiplicity in one timeless act where doing and knowing are identical.
claims.quote: A simple, eternal, God can do and know a vast multiplicity of things in one timeless act in which doing and knowing are the same.

claims.text: Because God is perfectly good, this simple God inevitably, though freely, does the best.
claims.quote: Being perfectly good, this simple God inevitably, though freely, does the best.

claims.text: Early on, divine simplicity was not seen as intuitively incompatible with trinitarian language.
claims.quote: In its early emergence, simplicity was not understood as posing intuitive incompatibilities with the development of trinitarian language.

claims.text: Divine simplicity deeply enriches the doxological dimension of trinitarian theology.
claims.quote: Simplicity deeply enriches the doxological dimension of trinitarian theology.

claims.text: Trinitarian theology will lose much doxological potential if the doctrine of divine simplicity is abandoned.
claims.quote: Trinitarian theology will lose a great deal of its doxological potential if we give up the doctrine of divine simplicity.

claims.text: The coherence of the doctrines of omnipresence and divine simplicity is called into question.
claims.quote: However, the coherence of the two doctrines are brought into question here.

claims.text: If both traditional omnipresence and divine simplicity are affirmed, the traditional model of omnipresence becomes incoherent.
claims.quote: If the traditional model of God’s omnipresence and divine simplicity are both affirmed, then the traditional model of God’s omnipresence is incoherent.

claims.text: There may be a potential way to harmonize omnipresence with divine simplicity.
claims.quote: Perhaps, however, there is some potential way of harmonizing the two.

claims.text: God’s essence enables predication of attributes, removing the need for constituent properties.
claims.quote: It proposes that God’s essence enables the predication of these attributes, eliminating the need for constituent properties.

claims.text: The truthmaker account overcomes ineffability while preserving divine simplicity.
claims.quote: The truthmaker account establishes a direct connection between God’s necessary existence and the truthfulness of statements about Him, overcoming the barrier of ineffability.

claims.text: The adequacy of formalizations of classical theistic doctrines has been disputed.
claims.quote: Moreover, the adequacy of such formalizations as such has, at least with respect to some classes of doctrines, been disputed.

claims.text: Most arguments against divine simplicity attributed to Plantinga were anticipated by al‑Ghazālī.
claims.quote: most of the argumentation against divine simplicity frequently credited to Plantinga had been nearly perfectly anticipated by al‑Ghazālī.

claims.text: Ghazālī’s new arguments remain valuable and informative for today’s discussion of divine simplicity.
claims.quote: Ghazālī develops ‘new’ arguments and moves that are still valuable and informative to the discussion of divine simplicity today.

claims.text: Throughout church history, multiple versions of divine simplicity existed, not only the Thomist version.
claims.quote: there have been different versions of divine simplicity throughout church history, though most current treatments focus on the Thomist version.

claims.text: Divine simplicity offers a more reliable monotheistic grounding for the Trinity than perichoresis.
claims.quote: the doctrine of divine simplicity provides a more reliable means of grounding the Trinity as monotheistic than the doctrine of perichoresis.

claims.text: Differences between contemporary and ancient treatments of divine simplicity stem from basic ontological differences.
claims.quote: many of the differences between contemporary and ancient treatments of divine simplicity boil down to more basic ontological differences.

claims.text: Gregory connects divine simplicity with the infinity proper to the divine nature.
claims.quote: Gregory links the divine simplicity with the infinity proper to the divine nature.

claims.text: For Gregory, the infinite and simple supreme being is the divine nature expressed in the Trinity, not the One.
claims.quote: for Gregory, the supreme being, who is infinite and simple, is not the One, but the divine nature as expressed in the three persons of the Trinity.

claims.text: Edwards claims that everything within God is God and that God has no constituent parts.

claims.text: By adopting divine simplicity, Edwards maintains God's unity in his Trinitarian theology.
claims.quote: 특히 하나님의 단순성 교리를 수용함으로써 하나님의 통일성이 확고히 유지될 수 있게 했다.

claims.text: Maimonides holds that God is absolutely simple, lacking composition, plurality, or accidental attributes.
claims.quote: Maimonides' philosophical system, particularly as articulated in *The Guide for the Perplexed*, asserts that God is absolutely simple, devoid of any composition, plurality, or accidental attributes.

claims.text: Therefore a purely apophatic approach is required, since any positive attribute would compromise God's unity.
claims.quote: This necessitates a purely apophatic approach to divine predication, where no positive attribute can be truly applied to God without compromising His unity and transcendence.

claims.text: Maimonides turns this paradox into a method that fosters intellectual humility and correct belief.
claims.quote: The paper argues that Maimonides transforms what appears to be a logical impasse into a sophisticated theological and philosophical method for cultivating intellectual humility and correct belief.

claims.text: Separating theology from economy assumes theology does not fundamentally arise from divine revelation.

claims.text: Irenaeus’ doctrine of divine simplicity is inseparable from the way God has revealed himself.
claims.quote: Behr argues that the last‑named answer is the only one that could befit Irenaeus.

claims.text: Simplicity undergirds traditional affirmations of God's aseity, immutability, infinity, eternality, perfection, and wisdom.
claims.quote: Van Mastricht chronicled how simplicity undergirds the traditional affirmations of God’s aseity, immutability, infinity, eternality, perfection and wisdom.

claims.text: If God is truly independent, his existence cannot depend on any constituent parts.
claims.quote: For example he argued that if God is a se, that is, truly independent and self-sufficient, God’s existence and nature cannot be dependent on any constituent parts.

claims.text: Thus divine simplicity occupies a controlling position in Reformed scholastic theology.
claims.quote: Virtually all the Reformed scholastic and Puritan theologies with which Edwards was familiar upheld divine simplicity.

claims.text: Aquinas’s strong doctrine of divine simplicity is vulnerable to modal collapse, eliminating real distinctions within God.
claims.quote: First, Aquinas’s view of a strong doctrine of divine simplicity is susceptible to modal collapse.

claims.text: The paper proposes a robust view of the divine Person that aligns with Scripture.
claims.quote: I will then offer a constructive and more robust view of the divine Person—one that aligns with the control of Scripture.

claims.text: The Mu‘tazila assert that divine attributes are identical with the divine essence.
claims.quote: The Mu‘tazila were the first Islamic thinkers to embrace the doctrine of divine simplicity, the idea that divine attributes are identical with divine essence.

claims.text: Abu al‑Hudhayl reduces essential attributes like knowledge and love to God the powerful, the agent of the best.
claims.quote: He reduces essential attributes, especially divine knowledge and divine love, to God the powerful, which he interprets as the agent of the best.

claims.text: Consequently, Mu‘tazilite divine simplicity reduces all attributes to the concept of God as the agent of the best.
claims.quote: This chapter argues that the Mu‘tazilite divine simplicity doctrine consists of reducing divine attributes to the concept of God as the agent of the best.

claims.text: Scotus and Ockham reveal tensions between divine simplicity and the multiplicity of attributes, action, and language.
claims.quote: Later scholastic philosophers such as John Duns Scotus and William Ockham exposed significant tensions and potential paradoxes when attempting to reconcile divine simplicity with the multiplicity of divine attributes, divine action in a complex world, and human linguistic limitations.

claims.text: Medieval debates highlighted the inherent limits of metaphysical explanation concerning a maximally simple God.
claims.quote: This study argues that the medieval debates surrounding divine simplicity served not only to refine theological understanding but also to delineate the inherent limits of metaphysical explanation itself.

claims.text: Divine simplicity suggests the divine essence is identical to actions such as knowing and willing.
claims.quote: The doctrine of divine simplicity as developed by Patristic writers suggests that the divine essence is identical to actions of the undivided divine nature, such as knowing and willing.

claims.text: Can operations of the divine essence be identical to the divine essence itself?
claims.quote: Can operations of the divine essence, whether in se or ad extra, be identical to the divine essence, to God’s very being?

claims.text: Divine simplicity posits that God is utterly without parts or internal composition.
claims.quote: The doctrine of divine simplicity, a cornerstone of classical theism, posits that God is utterly without parts or internal composition.

claims.text: Medieval debates on divine simplicity delineate the inherent limits of metaphysical explanation.
claims.quote: This paper argues that the medieval debates surrounding divine simplicity served not only to refine theological understanding but also to delineate the inherent limits of metaphysical explanation itself.

claims.text: Medieval critiques forced a reconsideration of the scope of philosophical tools applied to a maximally simple reality.
claims.quote: By analyzing the nuanced arguments concerning identity, distinction, and predication within the divine being, medieval critiques forced a reconsideration of the scope and efficacy of philosophical tools when applied to a maximally simple, transcendent reality.

claims.text: Divine simplicity is probably the most difficult aspect of classical theism to articulate satisfactorily.
claims.quote: In the last couple of decades the doctrine of divine simplicity, probably the aspect of classical theism most difficult to articulate in religiously and metaphysically satisfying terms, has returned to the centre of debates about the doctrine of God in systematic and philosophical theology.

claims.text: God is his own essence and existence, identical to each attribute, and pure act.
claims.quote: Duby seeks to present positive, scriptural arguments for the medieval doctrine of divine simplicity—that God is his own essence and existence, that he is identical to each of his attributes, and that he is pure act—and to defend the doctrine against the most powerful and common objections.

claims.text: Aquinas holds that God’s freedom includes alternate possibilities, allowing Him to do otherwise.
claims.quote: Further, he thinks that God’s freedom involves alternate possibilities: as He acts, it is in all respects open to Him to do otherwise.

claims.text: Because God is timeless, any alternative action must be possible in the same eternal present.
claims.quote: The possibility that He do otherwise must be one He could have realized in the same eternal present in which he actually acts.

claims.text: Maimonides asserts that God is absolutely simple, lacking composition, plurality, or accidental attributes.
claims.quote: Maimonides' philosophical system, particularly as articulated in The Guide for the Perplexed, asserts that God is absolutely simple, devoid of any composition, plurality, or accidental attributes.

claims.text: The apophatic paradox stems from the tension between human conceptualization of God and the need to negate such concepts.
claims.quote: The resulting "apophatic paradox" arises from the tension between the human need to conceptualize and speak about God, and the philosophical imperative to negate all such conceptualizations.

claims.text: Maimonides turns this paradox into a method that cultivates intellectual humility and correct belief.
claims.quote: The paper argues that Maimonides transforms what appears to be a logical impasse into a sophisticated theological and philosophical method for cultivating intellectual humility and correct belief.

claims.text: The study investigates whether a stable minimum meaning of divine simplicity persists in the Christian tradition.
claims.quote: This study investigates whether the Christian tradition nevertheless preserves a stable minimum meaning of simplicity.

claims.text: It distinguishes the anti‑assembly thesis from the stronger partlessness thesis regarding divine composition.
claims.quote: It distinguishes between two claims: the anti-assembly thesis, according to which God was never produced by combining prior elements, and the stronger partlessness thesis, according to which God possesses no intrinsic constituents at all.

claims.text: Across traditions, simplicity is consistently understood as excluding both assembly and intrinsic parthood.
claims.quote: The sources consistently treat simplicity as excluding both assembly and intrinsic parthood.

claims.text: Novatian’s doctrine of unified divine will, thought, and action draws directly from Irenaeus.
claims.quote: This article traces the influence of Irenaeus into the third century by arguing that Novatian’s argument regarding the unity of divine will, thought, and action (Novatian, De Trinitate 5-6) draws from Irenaeus (Contra Haereses 2.13 and 1.12).

claims.text: Novatian uses the same concepts, terms, and sequence as found in Irenaeus’s writings.
claims.quote: This article notes where, in this passage, Novatian uses the same concepts, terms, and sequence.

claims.text: If Novatian’s dependence on Irenaeus is correct, it shows Irenaeus’s influence on Ayre’s fourth theological trajectory that shaped Nicaea.
claims.quote: If this view of Novatian’s dependence is correct, it would demonstrate the influence of Irenaeus on the fourth of Lewis Ayre’s four theological trajectories that influenced Nicaea.

claims.text: Edwards’s strategies for individuating the persons of the Godhead are problematic.
claims.quote: In this paper I argue that Edwards's strategies for individuating the persons of the Godhead are problematic in several respects.

claims.text: Edwards distinguishes between 'real' and 'merely modal' distinctions within the Godhead.
claims.quote: Edwards also has an idiosyncratic (but not unorthodox) distinction between 'real' and 'merely modal' distinctions in the Godhead.

claims.text: His doctrine of the Trinity fails to resolve the tension with divine simplicity that he also endorses.
claims.quote: However, the most serious difficulty his doctrine of the Trinity fails to overcome concerns the relationship between the Triune persons and the doctrine of divine simplicity, both of which Edwards appears to endorse.

claims.text: Divine simplicity means God lacks any composition.
claims.quote: Cette étude souhaite contribuer à une meilleure connaissance et compréhension de l’idée de simplicité divine, qui signifie l’absence en Dieu de toute composition.

claims.text: Analytic philosophers have contested the coherence of divine simplicity.
claims.quote: Pièce centrale de la pensée théologique médiévale, elle fut redécouverte il y a 35 ans par des philosophes de tendance analytique, qui en contestèrent la cohérence.

claims.text: Divine simplicity serves as a powerful tool to open intelligence to a higher, mysterious yet luminous reality.
claims.quote: Loin d’apparaître comme incohérente, l’idée de simplicité divine est un outil puissant pour ouvrir notre intelligence à un plan de réalité supérieur, certes mystérieux, mais néanmoins lumineux.

claims.text: Aquinas concludes that in God essence and existence are identical.
claims.quote: Aquinas concludes from the first two that, in God, essence and existence are identical.

claims.text: The first objection in Summa Theologiae 3.4 leads this conclusion toward pantheism.
claims.quote: The first objection in Summa Theologiae 3.4 in effect leads this conclusion in a pantheistic direction.

claims.text: God’s existence differs from other beings by being pure actuality, whereas theirs are merely actual.
claims.quote: There is exactly one possible way in which God’s existence is different from the existence of everything else: God’s existence is pure actuality whereas the existence of everything else is actuality but not pure actuality.

claims.text: A major objection to divine simplicity is that it causes a modal collapse, eliminating contingency and making all truths necessary.
claims.quote: One of the most pressing objections against Divine simplicity is that it entails what is commonly termed a ‘modal collapse’, wherein all contingency is eliminated and every true proposition is rendered necessarily true.

claims.text: The common form of the modal collapse argument is famously invalid.
claims.quote: I show that a common form of this argument is in fact famously invalid.

claims.text: No repair of the argument avoids begging the question against divine simplicity.
claims.quote: I conclude that there is no clear way of repairing the argument that does not beg the question against the doctrine of Divine simplicity.

claims.text: Proponents claim divine simplicity makes all divine acts absolutely necessary, conflicting with divine freedom.
claims.quote: Proponents of the modal collapse argument claim that divine simplicity, traditionally conceived, contradicts other Christian commitments about divine freedom and grace by ultimately rendering all God’s acts, including creation and redemption, absolutely necessary.

claims.text: The modal collapse argument cannot generate the dilemma without additional premises.
claims.quote: the modal collapse argument is insufficient to generate this dilemma apart from additional premises

claims.text: These hidden premises are the real point of dispute.
claims.quote: these tacit premises are the true locus of dispute.

claims.text: The early fourteenth‑century emphasis on divine simplicity subtly shaped Wodeham’s and Chatton’s intra‑Trinitarian distinctions.
claims.quote: The paper argues that the strong emphasis on divine simplicity that emerged in the early fourteenth century had a subtle influence on how Wodeham and Chatton understood the intra-trinitarian distinctions between the Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

claims.text: Strong simplicity opposes God having positive attributes and threatens Trinitarian distinction.
claims.quote: Not only does the stronger doctrine of simplicity militate against God having positive attributes (such as wisdom and holiness), but it would seem to also eliminate the distinction between the persons of the Trinity.

claims.text: The doctrine of divine simplicity is motivated by the intuition that God is ontologically distinct from all beings.
claims.quote: The doctrine that God is free from any complexity is generally motivated by the intuition that God is ontologically distinct and therefore radically different from the rest of beings.

claims.text: Al‑Ghazālī mounts a philosophical attack on divine simplicity in his Incoherence of the Philosophers.
claims.quote: It was al‑Ghazālī to mount an attack against the idea of the divine simplicity in his Tahāfut al‑Falāsifa (The Incoherence of the Philosophers) where significant space is devoted to its refutation.

claims.text: Hinlicky’s work harshly critiques the Thomistic doctrine of divine simplicity.
claims.quote: He devotes his lengthy (70-page) second chapter to a review of the Thomistic version of it, and rather incessantly lambastes it throughout the book.

claims.text: The proof paradigm commits a category error by projecting finite, discursive proof onto the divine intellect.
claims.quote: We contend this argument is susceptible to a fundamental category error: it projects 'proof'—understood as a finite, discursive, and system‑relative creaturely epistemic tool—univocally onto the divine intellect.
