claims.quote: the positive reasons for upholding divine simplicity, and the bearing of divine simplicity on our view of the divine attributes.

claims.text: The Bible should be seen as ongoing divine speech without implying human control, grounded in divine simplicity and freedom.
claims.quote: this essay will characterize the Bible as ongoing divine speech within the context of a doctrine of God’s simplicity and freedom that will enable us to construe the canon of Scripture as written revelation without implying that human beings gain control of God’s revelatory work.

claims.text: Because God acts in the fullness of his indivisible essence, his communication in Scripture invariably exceeds the text itself.
claims.quote: in his simplicity, God always acts in the fullness of his being and by his indivisible, infinite essence, which means that in his communicative operation in Scripture God (or God’s action) invariably exceeds the text itself.

claims.text: In his simplicity, God is truly but never fully revealed to finite creatures.
claims.quote: in his simplicity, God is truly but never fully revealed to finite creatures who are unable to comprehend God’s singular plenitude.

claims.text: Divine simplicity is plausibly a biblical doctrine given standard scriptural derivation methods.
claims.quote: Divine simplicity is plausibly seen as a biblical doctrine, given a standard account of the way doctrine is derived from Scripture.

claims.text: Jeremiah 10’s polemic commits to a radical divine aseity that can plausibly infer divine simplicity.
claims.quote: I suggest this view of divine aseity might plausibly be thought to lead to the inference to divine simplicity.

claims.text: The appropriateness of reading Exodus 3:14 as supporting divine simplicity must be judged by scriptural judgments, not merely word semantics.
claims.quote: I begin this essay by arguing that the appropriateness of this interpretation of Exodus 3:14 should be evaluated by attention to the judgements about God made within scripture rather than merely the semantic range of a few words.

claims.text: The three questions of incomparability, intimacy, and ineffability allow a case for divine simplicity to unify these judgments.
claims.quote: Consideration of the kind of judgements these questions elicit about God allows a case to be made for the aptness of divine simplicity to hold the judgements together.

claims.text: Barrett’s account of divine simplicity is both biblical and consistent with the Christian doctrine of the Trinity.
claims.quote: The aim is to show that his account of the doctrine of divine simplicity is both biblical and consistent with the Christian doctrine of the Trinity.

claims.text: The modal collapse argument claims that absolute simplicity and necessity make creation absolutely necessary, collapsing God and creation into a single modal category.
claims.quote: The modal collapse argument claims that if God is both absolutely simple and absolutely necessary, then God’s act of creation is absolutely necessary, and therefore, the existence of the created world is also absolutely necessary.

claims.text: Islamic Neoplatonic thought distinguishes ontological, dependent, and logical necessity, avoiding modal collapse.
claims.quote: First, the modal collapse objection is based on a possible worlds framework whose concept of necessity is overly broad; this framework fails to distinguish between God as ontologically necessary in Himself, created being as dependently necessary through another, and mere logical necessity, all of which are recognized by Ibn Sina and Islamic thinkers.

claims.text: All classical and neo‑classical theists must accept a modally necessary creation because libertarian will models entail contingent effects.
claims.quote: Finally, I argue that all classical and neo‑classical theists must embrace a modally necessary creation because libertarian models of God’s will entail uncaused and brutely contingent effects.

claims.text: A God who creates ex nihilo cannot be composite.
claims.quote: The heart of my argument will be to (1) advance a historically-informed conception of creation ex nihilo, and (2) deduce that from such a notion of creation ex nihilo, that a God who creates ex nihilo cannot be composite.

claims.text: The argument avoids assuming that a composite God's existence depends on its parts.
claims.quote: I will ... not (1) arguing that a composite God’s existence would be dependent upon its parts and must be rejected, nor (2) made with a host of controversial metaphysical assumptions.

claims.text: The argument presupposes only modest metaphysical commitments.
claims.quote: I will presuppose modest metaphysical commitments and argue for DDS on the grounds of creation ex nihilo.

claims.text: Theists should embrace modal collapse, claiming the multiverse of worthy universes is the only possible world.
claims.quote: theists should maintain that the actual world is a multiverse featuring all and only universes worthy of being created and sustained by God, and – more controversially – it recommends that theists embrace modal collapse: the claim that this multiverse is the only possible world.

claims.text: If God exists in every possible world, then God exists in very bad worlds, making God culpable.
claims.quote: if God exists in every world, then God exists in those, too. And if God exists in very bad worlds, some say, God is culpable for not ensuring that they are better.

claims.text: The problem of possible evil argues that the possibility of bad worlds is evidence against theism.
claims.quote: The problem of possible evil claims that the possibility of bad worlds constitutes evidence against theism.

claims.text: ADS is claimed to imply a modal collapse, i.e., that God’s creation is absolutely necessary.
claims.quote: It is claimed that ADS implies a modal collapse, i.e. that God’s creation is absolutely necessary.

claims.text: Understanding the modal collapse argument leads ADS proponents to reject the premise that the same identical cause brings about the same effect.
claims.quote: I argue that a proper way of understanding the modal collapse argument naturally leads the proponent of ADS to reject a particular premise of the argument: namely, “the same identical cause brings about the same effect.”

claims.text: Rejecting that premise creates an explanatory gap concerning indeterminism in an absolutely simple God.
claims.quote: It leads to an explanatory gap: how can we explain the relevant type of indeterminism in an absolutely simple God?

claims.text: If the modal collapse argument succeeds, it entails a moral collapse where ethical principles fail.
claims.quote: the success of the modal collapse argument entails a moral collapse wherein well-established principles of ethical reasoning fail.

claims.text: Mullins’s modal collapse argument can be modified to survive its strongest rejoinder.
claims.quote: one can modify the argument to survive its most forceful rejoinder.

claims.text: Katherine Rogers’s appeal to a theistic multiverse does not defeat the moral collapse objection.
claims.quote: this manoeuvre proves ineffective against the moral collapse objection.

claims.text: Mullins’s modal collapse argument assumes a crucial term is rigid, rendering the argument invalid or question‑begging.
claims.quote: Mullins’s version of this argument assumes that a crucial term occurring within its premises is rigid, leaving the argument invalid or question begging.

claims.text: The test for discerning rigidity that Mullins adopts is false.
claims.quote: I argue that this test is false and then provide a new test.

claims.text: The new test undermines modal collapse arguments in general.
claims.quote: My test bodes ill for modal collapse arguments in general.

claims.text: Gödel’s ontological system intends modal collapse as a consequence, aligning with his philosophical views.
claims.quote: Gödel’s texts confirm modal collapse as intended consequence of his ontological system.

claims.text: In Gödel’s framework, modality and time should be derived from the fundamental concept of cause.
claims.quote: the concepts of modality and time should be derived in terms of the “fundamental philosophical concept” of cause.

claims.text: Modal collapse should be seen as a rise of modalities to the perfect being, not a deficit.
claims.quote: modal collapse should not be conceived in Gödel so much as a deficit, but rather as a kind of the rise of modalities to the “perfect” being.

claims.text: Hintikka interprets Aristotle as committed to a Principle of Plenitude that no genuine possibility remains unactualized over infinite time.
claims.quote: On Jaakko Hintikka’s understanding of Aristotle’s modal thought, Aristotle is committed to a version of the Principle of Plenitude, which is the thesis that no genuine possibility will go unactualized in an infinity of time.

claims.text: Aristotle can accept a de re version of the Principle of Plenitude that permits genuine unactualized possibilities.
claims.quote: I show how Aristotle may accept a form of the Principle of Plenitude that allows for genuine unactualized possibilities in the world.

claims.text: Tomaszewski claims modal collapse arguments against divine simplicity are invalid because they illicitly substitute non‑rigid singular terms in intensional contexts.

claims.quote: the theologian represents a conception of God in which divine perfection manifests in an outpouring of love.

claims.text: Prange proves that the election controversy is not so settled that further historical study is unnecessary.
claims.quote: Prange proves this wrong in his superb retelling of it.

claims.text: Farley's theory of tragic existence and divine compassion is distressing and depressing.
claims.quote: I find Farley's theory of tragic existence and divine compassion distressing and depressing.

claims.text: The tragic vision presented sheds no real light on the problem of suffering.
claims.quote: her tragic vision sheds no real light on the problem of suffering.

claims.text: The paper proves that God exists using pure mathematics such as category theory, modal logic, and model theory.
claims.quote: This paper proves that God exists using pure mathematics—specifically, category theory, modal logic, and model theory.

claims.text: Every coherent definition of God must contain the three features: existence & uniqueness, necessity, and maximality.
claims.quote: every coherent god-definition must contain exactly three essential features: Existence & Uniqueness (E): There is exactly one god Necessity (N): God exists necessarily (cannot fail to exist) Maximality (M): God has all perfections to the maximum degree

claims.text: Deriving necessity from maximality avoids circular reasoning in the proof of God’s existence.
claims.quote: This derivation—from maximality to necessity—is crucial because it avoids the circular reas

claims.text: The cost sharing system in the Kenduri ceremony is regulated by customary agreements and involves three main parties.
claims.quote: The results of the study indicate that the cost sharing system in the Kenduri ceremony is regulated based on customary agreements and involves three main parties, namely ase kae (nuclear family), children of rona (siblings), and children of wina (sisters).

claims.text: Cost accountability is shown in the family deliberation mechanism where all contributions and expenditures are recorded openly.
claims.quote: Cost accountability is reflected in the family deliberation mechanism, where every contribution and expenditure is recorded and accounted for openly.

claims.text: Cost accountability functions economically and symbolically, strengthening solidarity and collective responsibility among the Manggarai people.
claims.quote: This study concludes that cost accountability in the kenduri ceremony not only functions economically, but also become a symbol of the spiritual, social, and cultural values of the Manggarai people which strengthen solidarity and collective responsibility.

claims.text: Philosophers defending divine simplicity and theologians rejecting it both agree its heritage is Greek, not biblical.
claims.quote: Philosophers of religion who defend it and theologians who dismiss it agree on its Greek, rather than biblical, heritage.

claims.text: A Christian account of divine simplicity, as in Thomas, keeps a Creator‑creature distinction grounded in the Trinity and Incarnation.
claims.quote: On the contrary, a particularly Christian account of divine simplicity, as reflected for example in Thomas, maintains a Creator‑creature distinction as understood in light of Trinity and Incarnation.

claims.text: The modern follower of Thomas on simplicity is Barth, not Stump and Kretzmann.
claims.quote: The true modern follower of Thomas on simplicity is not Stump and Kretzmann, but Barth.

claims.text: Swinburne treats simplicity as a property of the theistic hypothesis, whereas Aquinas treats it as a property of God.
claims.quote: However, Swinburne takes simplicity as a property of the theistic hypothesis, while for Aquinas simplicity is a property of God himself.

claims.text: For Swinburne, simpler theories are, ceteris paribus, more likely to be true.
claims.quote: For Swinburne, simpler theories are ceteris paribus more likely to be true;

claims.text: Despite their differences, the paper highlights previously unnoticed parallels between Aquinas’s and Swinburne’s thoughts.
claims.quote: Notwithstanding their different approaches, some unreckoned parallels between their thoughts are brought to light.

claims.text: Natural theology is shaped by prior metaphysical and epistemological commitments, not a neutral method.
claims.quote: This article argues that natural theology is not a neutral or self-contained method for establishing theological conclusions but is inherently shaped by prior metaphysical and epistemological commitments.

claims.text: The First Way does not necessarily lead to divine simplicity because its premises can be challenged.
claims.quote: While the transition from an unmoved mover to simplicity is logically coherent within this framework, the article contends that the First Way itself does not necessitate these conclusions.

claims.text: Natural theology should be seen as part of an interdependent system with epistemology, metaphysics, and theology proper.
claims.quote: The article concludes that natural theology must be understood as part of a broader, interdependent system in which epistemology, metaphysics, natural theology, and theology proper mutually inform one another, rather than as an independent foundation for determining the nature of God.

claims.text: Critics argue Aquinas’s view of eternity and immutability relies on a misconceived Platonism, making his simplicity a sophistry.
claims.quote: Some critics, while praising Aquinas on many counts, have concluded that his view of God’s eternity and immutability depends upon a misconceived Platonism, consequently, his explanations of God’s so-called “simplicity” are based on sophistry and illusion.

claims.text: I defend Aquinas’s views as a coherent whole, showing development and greater use of metaphor in his later works.
claims.quote: Against this, I present Aquinas’s views as the coherent whole I believe them to be, his later works showing some development as well as greater indulgence in metaphor.

claims.text: Their disagreements about God stem from a metaphysical dispute over whether being is a composition.
claims.quote: I claim that their disagreements about God occur because of a metaphysical disagreement on whether being constitutes a composition.

claims.text: Plotinus assumes unity is most fundamental, whereas Aquinas assumes being is most fundamental.
claims.quote: Plotinus thinks it does, and assumes that unity is most fundamental, whereas Aquinas thinks it does not, and assumes that being is most fundamental.

claims.text: Plotinus’ position is inferior to Aquinas due to the unintelligibility and inconsistency of the One as the source of being.
claims.quote: I argue that Plotinus' position is inferior to Aquinas due to unintelligibility and inconsistency of the One as the source of being and unrelated to being, while also attacking Plotinus' analogies for it.

claims.text: Scotus holds that God’s existence can be rationally proved.
claims.quote: Scotus clearly holds that God’s existence can be rationally proved.

claims.text: For Scotus, God’s existence is the goal of metaphysics.
claims.quote: God’s existence is the goal of metaphysics; so there is a crucial sense in which someone doing metaphysics is, for Scotus, doing natural theology.

claims.text: For Aquinas, the identity of essence and existence proves God’s simplicity.
claims.quote: The identity of essence and existence is for Thomas a proof of the simplicity of God (though at times he argues identity of essence and existence on the basis of simplicity).

claims.text: Aquinas describes God as simple and as essential being.
claims.quote: This paper has the modest goal of exploring Thomas Aquinas' description of God as simple and as essential being.

claims.text: Divine ideas are ontologically identical to the divine essence.
claims.quote: according to which the divine ideas are ontologically identical to the divine essence.

claims.text: Divine ideas must have real ontological relations to their objects to serve as extrinsic formal causes.
claims.quote: the divine ideas need real ontological relations to their respective objects in the world in order to function as extrinsic formal causes.

claims.text: Analytic philosophers who reject divine simplicity are not correct.
claims.quote: I shall shortly suggest that they are not.

claims.text: The doctrine that God is entirely simple has been a longstanding teaching in Christianity.
claims.quote: That God is entirely simple is a teaching that has been reiterated by generations of Christians.

claims.text: Daily language is insufficient for directly speaking about God because of divine simplicity.
claims.quote: The most important claim of the thesis of the divine simplicity is that the daily expressions of language, which are constructed in reference to the material and composite beings, are not deep enough in the meaning, to the degree that one may not directly use them when talking about God.

claims.text: What degree does the resemblance of created beings to the final cause permit us to speak about God?
claims.quote: What kind and to what degree the resemblance of the caused beings to the final cause (God) “ a resemblance that they possess in their natures “ allows human beings to talk about the final cause.

claims.text: Contemporary discussions often misinterpret Aquinas’s divine simplicity by ignoring his triplex via theology.
claims.quote: few contemporary discussions notice the way Aquinas employs pseudo-Dionysius’s triplex via as a principled heuristic that governs and organizes his theological inquiries concerning divine simplicity.

claims.text: Two problems for classical theism cannot be solved by perfect being theology or Thomistic accounts that omit TVT.
claims.quote: In the first part I introduce two problems for CT that cannot be resolved by PBT and Thomistic accounts of DDS that omit Aquinas’s TVT.

claims.text: Thomistic triplex via theology offers a fertile alternative to perfect being theology for addressing these problems.
claims.quote: I show that, like Aquinas’s DDS, the value of Thomist TVT extends beyond historical exegesis and provides exponents of CT with a fertile alternative to the more well-known Anselmian-inspired heuristic of perfect being theology.

claims.text: Thomistic participation expresses the dependence relation of creatures to God.
claims.quote: Thomistic participation is most properly understood as the expression of the dependence relation of creatures to God, a relation exemplified by a metaphysical structure open to analysis by the thinker sufficiently trained in the general science of created being (metaphysics).

claims.text: For Aquinas, creation means everything except God is creature and the creaturely nature saturates the world.
claims.quote: For Aquinas, creation means that all but God is creature, and that the creaturely nature of the world definitively saturates the world and everything in it.

claims.text: Aquinas concludes that God is both transcendent and immanent, so the world is under divine governance yet free.
claims.quote: By means of an analysis of the metaphysical structure of being and beings in terms of participation Aquinas arrives at a conception of a God who, as the first and supreme cause of the world, is both transcendent of it and immanent in it, such that the world is a manifold of created natures at once utterly under divine governance and free in their own order.

claims.text: Long shows that Thomas’s first forty‑three questions form a single doctrine of God linking the one and the triune.
claims.quote: Long convincingly demonstrates that, for Thomas, the first forty‑three questions in fact constitute a single doctrine of God, according to which "de deo uno must be read from the perspective of de deo trino, and de deo trino must be read from the perspective of de deo uno" (xxii).

claims.text: The classical approach does not pit divine simplicity against the Trinity but affirms God as perfectly simple and triune.
claims.quote: the classical approach to the doctrine of God, which dominated the history of Christian thought up to the early eighteenth century, does not pit divine simplicity against the divine trinity, but acknowledges God as perfectly simple and triune.

claims.text: The examined Trinitarian conceptions fail to satisfy the demands of simplicity and logic better than Arianism.
claims.quote: We will eventually conclude that these conceptions do not fulfill the demands of simplicity and logic better than Arianism (an unorthodox conception).

claims.text: Therefore Arianism is the better option for the rational theist.
claims.quote: Subsequently we will argue that Arianism is the better option, given the alternatives, for the rational theist.

claims.text: Aquinas holds that God’s external acts correspond to God’s internal being, while Barth holds they correspond to God’s internal acts.
claims.quote: Aquinas maintains that God’s external acts correspond to God’s internal being, whereas Barth maintains that God’s external acts correspond to God’s internal acts" (16).

claims.text: Wittman treats divine simplicity as a negative doctrine preventing God from being reduced to a thing among things.
claims.quote: Wittman emphasizes that divine “simplicity” is a negative doctrine whose purpose is to ensure that we do not reduce God to a thing among other things.

claims.text: The paper substitutes a logical consequence of divine simplicity for Aquinas’s actual explanation.
claims.quote: I argue that the paper substitutes a logical consequence of God's simplicity for Aquinas' explanation, and fails to deliver the explanation it promises of why there is no real distinction between the suppositionally necessary features of God and the absolutely necessary ones.

claims.text: Divine simplicity is neither necessary nor sufficient for the conclusions of the applications discussed.
claims.quote: I suggest the doctrine of divine simplicity is, strictly, neither necessary nor sufficient for the conclusions of the "applications."

claims.text: The book aims to present a God who exceeds all we can think and is not a product of our thoughts.
claims.quote: God without Parts intends to tell us about the God who is in no way the product of our thoughts but rather exceeds all we can think.

claims.text: Alston’s orthodox interpretation of Aquinas’s analogia is more faithful to Aquinas’s text than Wolterstorff’s heterodoxy.
claims.quote: I show why Alston's "orthodox" interpretation is more faithful to the letter of Aquinas's text than is Wolterstorff's "heterodoxy".

claims.text: Geiger maintains that Aquinas’s doctrine of divine ideas is integral to sustaining divine simplicity while allowing God intimate awareness of creation.
claims.quote: Geiger maintains that the doctrine of divine ideas is integral to Aquinas's theological thinking—indeed, so integral that Thomas needs to posit divine ideas in order to sustain the divine simplicity while simultaneously allowing for God's intimate awareness of each aspect of his creation.

claims.text: God’s existence can be demonstrated by unaided human reason.
claims.quote: In fact, the traditional conviction that God's existence is demonstrable by unaided human reason (demonstration here understood according to the Scholastic sense, “that the conclusion that God exists follows with necessity or deductive validity from premises that are certain, where the certainty of the premises can in turn be shown via metaphysical analysis”) is not difficult to come by.

claims.text: Feser’s book provides an exposition and defense of important arguments for God’s existence that Aquinas did not discuss.
claims.quote: According to Feser, the book answers to “a need for an exposition and defense of certain important arguments for God's existence that Aquinas himself does not discuss and which have also received insufficient attention in recent work in natural theology” (10).

claims.text: In Aquinas, divine ideas function as exemplars that causally produce created things.
claims.quote: According to Thomas, the ideas in the mind of God are not only principles of his knowledge, but they are productive principles as well. In this role, God's ideas act as exemplars for things that he creates.

claims.text: Aquinas’s exemplarism explains the existence and order of the created universe.
claims.quote: As Doolan shows, this theory of exemplarism is an integral part of Thomas's account of the existence and order of the created universe.

claims.text: The Molinist free‑will defense fails because middle knowledge must be rejected.
claims.quote: I argue that the Molinist version fails, because we have reason to reject its doctrine of Middle Knowledge.

claims.text: If God causes our actions, the free‑will defense is untenable.
claims.quote: This thesis provides an additional reason to reject the Free Will Defense.

claims.text: Aquinas’s doctrine of divine causality is compatible with libertarian human freedom and avoids theological determinism.
claims.quote: I maintain, on the contrary, that Aquinas's views do not commit him to theological determinism. Not only are his views compatible with a libertarian conception of human freedom...

claims.text: Aquinas cannot reconcile absolute simplicity with the doctrines of the Trinity and the Incarnation.
claims.quote: Christopher Hughes argues that Aquinas fails in his attempt to reconcile absolute simplicity with the doctrines of the Trinity and the Incarnation.

claims.text: An absolutely simple God cannot exist because it lacks any structure.
claims.quote: According to Hughes, an absolutely simple God is an impossibility, a being too lacking in structure to exist.

claims.text: The Identity Thesis follows from basic theism and does not make God an abstract object.
claims.quote: This paper shows that the Identity Thesis follows from a basic theistic belief and does not render God abstract.

claims.text: From the Identity Thesis one can formulate a new ontological argument for God.
claims.quote: It also discusses how one might move from the Identity Thesis to the full doctrine of divine simplicity and shows that the Identity Thesis generates a new ontological argument.

claims.text: God’s personal relations are distinct from each other but not from the divine substance.
claims.quote: The article concludes that while God's personal relations are really distinct from each other, there is no real distinction between the personal relations and the divine substance.

claims.text: The Trinity is compatible with the doctrine of divine simplicity.
claims.quote: the Trinity and the doctrine of divine simplicity are thus agreeable.

claims.text: Divine simplicity makes sense and is useful for speaking about God.
claims.quote: that this idea of divine "simplicity" does make sense and is useful for talk about God

claims.text: Divine simplicity supports moderate, if not overwhelming, claims for analogical predication in faith.
claims.quote: that it does lend support to temperate, if not to overpowering claims about the need for analogical predication in matters of faith

claims.text: When separated from each other and Hellenistic baggage, simplicity and analogy are philosophically manageable and helpful for plain religious lives.
claims.quote: that, when distinguished from each other and from some Hellenistic metaphysical baggage, the notions of simplicity and analogy are both philosophically manageable and helpful within plain, if theologically inquisitive, religious lives

claims.text: Critics misunderstand the De Deo Uno’s purpose; it guides religious language rather than defining God.
claims.quote: these critics misunderstand the purpose of the De Deo Uno; it is meant to be a guide for what language we use about God, not a definitive definition for Him

claims.text: Critics overlook Aquinas’s point that God’s essence is unknowable because He exceeds human comprehension.
claims.quote: these critics also overlook the very topic Aquinas stressed the most: we can never truly know God’s essence because God is beyond our abilities to comprehend

claims.text: The originative principle of law is simple in itself while generating manifold derivative forms of law.
claims.quote: the originative principle of law remains simple in itself while proceeding out of itself in its generation of manifold derivative forms of law

claims.text: God is a law to Himself in divine simplicity and a law to creatures, distinguishing first and second eternal law.
claims.quote: He distinguishes between a first and a second eternal law on the ground that God is a law both to himself (in se) in his divine simplicity and to all creatures besides (ad extra)

claims.text: According to Aquinas, we can only know what God is not, not what He is.
claims.quote: we can only know what God is not, rather than what he is

claims.text: God is pure form, his nature, and his substance is his existence.
claims.quote: God is pure form and he is his nature, so that the substance of God is his existence

claims.text: We may analogically express God, but we cannot name Him.
claims.quote: I close by arguing that we may analogically express God, but cannot name Him

claims.text: We can understand God’s unity before differentiable otherness by grasping it in terms of potential.
claims.quote: we may understand God’s Unity prior to differentiable otherness by understanding in terms of potential

claims.text: The proof for the real distinction is incomplete because it fails to ground its major premise.
claims.quote: the proof as it stands is incomplete, not in failing to offer a conclusion, but in failing to ground its major premise

claims.text: Is the real distinction a deduction from God’s simplicity or an insight drawn from experience?
claims.quote: Is the distinction a deduction we make from our knowledge of God’s essence, or an insight drawn from our experience

claims.text: Bonaventure holds that angels must be composed of matter and form to protect divine simplicity.
claims.quote: For Bonaventure, in order to protect the uniqueness of divine simplicity it is imperative to hold that angels, like all other created beings, are composed of matter and form as diverse natures.

claims.text: Aquinas claims pure spirits are composed of two distinct principles, essence and esse, related as potency and act.
claims.quote: For Thomas Aquinas, purely spiritual beings cannot be composed of matter and form but must be composed of two really distinct principles essence and esse which are related to one another as potency and act.

claims.text: Godfrey argues that angels need not be posited with two distinct principles to avoid being as simple as God.
claims.quote: For Godfrey, ... there is no need to posit two really distinct principles of being or two distinct natures in angels in order to avoid making them as simple as God himself.

claims.text: The author contends that Aquinas’s doctrine of ideas is a key to understanding his metaphysics.
claims.quote: His contention is that, although Thomas’s doctrine of ideas is perhaps not the key to an understanding of his metaphysics, it is certainly “a key to such an understanding” (xiv).

claims.text: Doolan establishes that Aquinas affirmed a multiplicity of divine ideas, contrary to Gilson’s view.
claims.quote: Doolan first establishes, against Gilson and others, that Aquinas did indeed hold that there was a multiplicity of divine ideas.

claims.text: Doolan concludes that ideas exist merely as known beings, not as real ones, allowing many of them.
claims.quote: “It is for this reason,” Doolan concludes, “that the ideas exist simply as known beings rather than as real ones and, moreover, that there can be many of them” (110).

claims.text: Dawkins argues that anything complex enough to create an organism must itself have been designed.
claims.quote: anything complex enough to create an organism must itself have been designed.

claims.text: The soundness of Dawkins’s argument depends on his use of Aquinas’s First Way.
claims.quote: The validity of this argument rests on Dawkins’ use of Thomas Aquinas’ First Way.

claims.text: Aquinas is indebted to Avicenna for formulating divine simplicity in relation to the essence‑existence distinction.
claims.quote: he is nevertheless indebted to Avicenna's philosophy in formulating how divine simplicity is to be understood in relation to the essence-existence distinction, to arguments of God's existence, and to other metaphysical issues in general.

claims.text: Avicenna’s view that God is simple follows from his proof of God’s necessary existence.
claims.quote: Avicenna’s view of God’s simplicity is an implication of his proof of God’s necessary existence.

claims.text: Aquinas is both formally and materially indebted to Avicenna for his doctrine of God’s unity and simplicity.
claims.quote: Aquinas, ... is both formally and materially indebted to Avicenna as regards to formulating God’s unity and simplicity

claims.text: The nature of Aquinas’s analogy depends on whether he works within an Aristotelian or Platonic epistemological framework.
claims.quote: It will become evident during this discussion that the issue of the nature of analogy hinges on the wider issue of how far Aquinas is working within an Aristotelian or a Platonic framework of epistemology.

claims.text: Cardinal Cajetan was the first to divide analogy into several distinct types.
claims.quote: Cardinal Cajetan (1469−1534) in his De Nominum analogia (1498) was the first to divide analogy into various types.

claims.text: Cajetan claimed that in the analogy of attribution a univocal term relates differently to each analogate.
claims.quote: Similarly Cajetan thought that in the 'analogy of attribution' a univocal term shares a different relationship with each of the analogates.

claims.text: God is perfect and simple, which entails having no physical or metaphysical parts or temporal stages.
claims.quote: Unlike all other beings, God is perfect and simple. Simplicity entails that God has no physical or metaphysical parts or temporal stages.

claims.text: The book replies that God is the creator and conserver of everything that exists.
claims.quote: The book replies that God is the creator and conserver of all else that exists.

claims.text: The book argues that God may have created a world whose goodness matches the capacities of its creatures.
claims.quote: The book argues, rather, that God may have created a world whose goodness matches the capacities of its creatures.

claims.text: St. Thomas held that spiritual substances such as souls and angels do not contain matter, unlike Avicebron and other Neoplatonists.
claims.quote: Unlike the Spanish philosopher Avicebron and all the Neoplatonists , St. Thomas held that spiritual substances (human souls and angels) do not include matter.

claims.text: Thomas argues that every essence can be understood without any knowledge of its existence.
claims.quote: every essence can be understood without knowing anything about its existence.

claims.text: MacIntosh aims to demonstrate to contemporary philosophers unfamiliar with Aquinas that he is of philosophical importance.
claims.quote: He wishes to show contemporary philosophers unfamiliar with Aquinas that he is of philosophical importance.

claims.text: The book aims to gather, explain, and synthesize Thomas’s ideas on the extasis amoris.
claims.quote: The purpose of this book, which is based on the author's doctoral dissertation, is "to gather together, to explain, and to synthesize Thomas's ideas on the extasis amoris," which he describes as "a bright gem in the crown of his philosophy of love."

claims.text: Modern caricatures of Thomas as a dry, barren, technical thinker are deflated by the author’s description of love’s paradox.
claims.quote: Modern caricatures of Thomas as a dry, barren, and technical thinker are deflated in the author's description of the principal paradox of amor in Thomas's works as "the lived reality of going out of oneself to the other in a self-forgetful oblation or surrender that is also, and for the same reason, the height of self-perfection."

claims.text: Arguments for God’s existence have been presented since Aristotle.
claims.quote: Arguments for the existence of God go back at least to Aristotle, who argued that there must be a first mover, itself unmoved.

claims.text: An infinite series of moved beings is impossible; therefore a first unmoved mover must exist.
claims.quote: It is impossible, however, that there should be an infinite series of moved and moving beings; hence there must be a first unmoved mover.

claims.text: Weinandy argues that the risen Christ remains a man who possesses joy, compassion, and love.
claims.quote: He puts forward the thesis that the risen and glorious Christ "is still a man, and thus still possesses the human emotions of joy, compassion and love" (252 n. 18).

claims.text: Weinandy asks whether, as a risen man, Christ’s love continues to grow through his deeds of love.
claims.quote: Weinandy wonders whether "as a risen man, Christ's love is not continuing to grow since ... he continues to enact deeds of love on our behalf" (255 n. 24).

claims.text: Recent defenses of divine simplicity have failed to meet the analogical language challenge, making their arguments null‑and‑void.
claims.quote: This essay’s aim is to demonstrate how recent defenses of divine simplicity have failed to address the prevailing challenge of analogical language, and thereby render much of their argumentation for simplicity’s appropriateness in Christian theology null-and-void.

claims.text: Cajetan’s analogical positions do not provide a sufficient framework to ground intelligible propositions about a simple God.
claims.quote: Finally, the third section critiques the kinds of analogical positions found in Thomas Cajetan’s influential De Nominum Analogia, showing that they do not provide a sufficient analogical framework to ground intelligible propositions or inferences about a simple God, which thereby places the original three authors’ defenses in danger of serious incoherence.

claims.text: Aquinas consistently distinguishes the angelic person (supposit) from its nature.
claims.quote: Yet, as this paper argues, Aquinas consistently puts forward just such a distinction.

claims.text: Recognizing this distinction illuminates Aquinas’s view of divine simplicity and act‑potency in creatures.
claims.quote: It is important to recognize the distinction between supposit and nature in angels not only for its own sake as it touches on his understanding of created persons—human or angelic—but also insofar as it sheds light on Aquinas’s understanding of divine simplicity and of other act‑potency compositions in creatures.

claims.text: Emery situates Thomas’s doctrine within medieval theology and links it to patristic debates.
claims.quote: Emery places Thomas's doctrine within medieval theology and demonstrates its relation to the patristic debates, which Thomas knew well.

claims.text: Emery aims to connect the immanent Trinity with its economic effect on human salvation.
claims.quote: Overall Emery seeks to link harmoniously the speculative doctrine of the Trinity in itself (immanent) to the Trinity's effectuation of man's salvation (economic).

claims.text: God is perfect and simple, unlike any other being.
claims.quote: The account that I offer maintains that God, unlike all other beings, is perfect and simple.

claims.text: Philosophical critics doubt the logical plausibility and religious accuracy of this account.
claims.quote: Philosophical critics may have doubts about the tenability of this account, both as a matter of logical plausibility and as a matter of religious accuracy.

claims.text: I believe several doubts are dispelled in the following chapters.
claims.quote: It would be rash of me to claim to quell all reasonable doubts. But I believe that several of them are dispelled in the chapters that follow, and I am eager to entertain new doubts.

claims.text: Divine simplicity is an often misunderstood claim that makes God’s goodness essential to His being, not merely an action.
claims.quote: Chapter one opens with discussions of divine simplicity (an often misunderstood theological claim) that call for the goodness of God and understand that goodness to be essential to God’s own being-ness (chs. two and three explicitly develop this theme) and not simply something God does (expounded in ch. four).

claims.text: Holmes offers a Thomistic response to Barth’s dialectical use of divine simplicity.
claims.quote: As part of his project, Holmes also offers a Thomistic counter to Barth’s own dialectical appropriation of divine simplicity (pp. 23–27).

claims.text: Creation is presented as the enactment of God’s goodness.
claims.quote: Chapter five offers a view of creation as the goodness of God enacted, carrying the reader into ch. six on issues of goodness and evil in light of the foregoing discussions of God’s goodness.

claims.text: If there is a plurality of relation in God, something can be enumerated, which challenges divine unity.
claims.quote: If there is a plurality of relation in God, there is something that can be enumerated, says Thomas.

claims.text: Aquinas distinguishes absolute plurality from relational unity to preserve divine simplicity.
claims.quote: He distinguishes between "absolute" plurality and the mutually definitory relations of the Trinitarian life which rule out any "composition" in God.

claims.text: Cross’s methodological and historical approaches make the Subtle Doctor accessible to analytically trained readers.
claims.quote: Cross’s methodological and historical approaches enable him to introduce the Subtle Doctor to readers who, while familiar with the approach of analytic philosophy, may not be familiar with the riches of medieval philosophical theology.

claims.text: The book provides some of the clearest explications of Duns Scotus’s thought.
claims.quote: His sustained analysis of particular texts offer some of the clearest explications one finds in work on Duns Scotus.

claims.text: Balthasar asks how the crucified Christ can serve as an icon of a beautiful God.
claims.quote: In the first volume of The Glory of the Lord, Hans Urs von Balthasar asks how the crucified Christ can be considered an icon of a beautiful God.

claims.text: Placing the cross at the centre of aesthetics forces a rethink of divine simplicity, being, beauty, and love.
claims.quote: By placing the cross at the centre of intramundane aesthetics, Balthasar forces us to rethink, not only the meaning of the divine simplicity, but the relation in God among being, beauty and love.

claims.text: An analogy of genus or species cannot be applied to the Trinity because it conflicts with divine simplicity.
claims.quote: I will argue that ultimately an analogy of genus or species cannot properly be applied to the Trinity because it contradicts the doctrine of divine simplicity.

claims.text: Aquinas permits a limited Damascene‑style analogy to illuminate God’s unique communicability.
claims.quote: Aquinas does allow for a reading of Damascene similar to that of the Lombard, to the extent that, according to our limited mode of knowledge, the relationship of individuals to a species can help us to understand the mode of communicability unique to God’s essence.

claims.text: The thesis defends divine simplicity by showing Jenson’s trinitarian theology relies on its logic.
claims.quote: I am able to approach Jenson’s writing with a multivalent account of divine simplicity. This allows me to demonstrate various ways in which Jenson himself, despite several critical remarks about simplicity, actually deploys the logic or grammar of simplicity in a way that is integral to his trinitarian theology.

claims.text: Relational Emergence Theory asserts that the essence of the universe is neither matter, nor energy, nor information, but 'relation'.
claims.quote: This paper proposes "Relational Emergence Theory," which asserts that the essence of the universe is neither matter, nor energy, nor information, but "relation."

claims.text: Although this framework does not provide new observable predictions, it offers a meta-theory that delineates disciplinary boundaries, shows interconnections, and provides a naturalistic foundation for questions of human meaning.

claims.text: Worship-worthiness should be treated as the foundational question of philosophy of religion.
claims.quote: This paper argues that worship-worthiness should be treated as the foundational question of philosophy of religion.

claims.text: Worship-Worthiness Theology has axiological, prudential, and methodological priority over Non-Worship-Worthiness Theology—a thesis called Worship-Worthiness First.
claims.quote: I argue that WWT has axiological, prudential, and methodological priority over NWWT – a thesis I call Worship-Worthiness First.

claims.text: Worship-worthiness is not one topic among others; it should guide and structure all other philosophical questions.
claims.quote: Worship-worthiness, this paper argues, is not one topic among others. It is the question that should guide and structure all the others.

claims.text: The miraculous coin in the fish’s mouth is a Christological and providential narrative addressing a specific historical circumstance rather than establishing a normative doctrine of supernatural financial provision.
claims.quote: The analysis demonstrates that the miraculous coin in the fist’s mouth is primarily a Christological and providential narrative addressing a specific historical circumstance rather than establishing a normative doctrine of supernatural financial provision.

claims.text: While belief in divine miracles is rationally defensible within Christian theism, the doctrinal universalization of miracle money exceeds the hermeneutical intention of the Matthean text and lacks sufficient epistemic warrant.
claims.quote: While belief in divine miracles is rationally defensible within Christian theism, the doctrinal universalization of miracle money exceeds the hermeneutical intention of the Matthean text and lacks sufficient epistemic warrant.

claims.text: Priority polytheism reconciles belief in an ultimate divinity with a pantheon of gods by employing the priority monist view to make the ultimate divinity metaphysically prior.
claims.quote: I will propose a way of understanding how such views can work through engagement with the priority monist view in metaphysics, using this view to construct a version of polytheism called priority polytheism.

claims.text: Epistemological and theological truths, though distinct, can complement each other and play a vital role in flourishing human life.
claims.quote: The aim of this paper is to demonstrate, through comparative analysis, that although epistemological and theological truths are distinct, they can complement each other and can play a vital role in flourishing human life.

claims.text: Epistemology and theology use different methods and objectives, leading to different presentations of truth.
claims.quote: Epistemology and theology have advanced in the pursuit of truth with different methods and distinct objectives. Consequently, their presentations of truth also different.

claims.text: Bergson’s religion philosophy grounds itself in the concept of life, establishing a religious vitalism that converges with William James’s pragmatism.
claims.quote: We will then show that Bergson’s philosophy of religion, by grounding itself in the concept of life to capture the significance of religious experiences in human existence, lays the foundations for what could be called a religious vitalism, thereby engaging with and converging toward the thought of the American pragmatist philosopher William James.

claims.quote: The findings suggest that Qur'anic argument often treats clarity not as bare information but as an event of moral exposure.

claims.text: A structured coding model distinguishing evidential terms is needed to map how clarity becomes morally binding in Qur'anic discourse.

claims.text: A navigation system does not directly measure its destination but estimates the traveler’s relation to signals, history, landmarks, uncertainty, and possible paths, correcting movement over time.
claims.quote: Its governing distinction is that a navigation system does not directly measure its destination. It estimates the traveler’s changing relation to signals, history, landmarks, uncertainty, and possible paths, then corrects movement over time.

claims.text: The same general capacities used to move through physical environments also support navigation through ideas, relationships, values, traditions, rituals, and represented futures.

claims.text: Biology alone does not determine which destination is true or good.
claims.quote: The body supplies the capacity to receive, remember, estimate, map, and correct, but biology alone does not determine which destination is true or good.

claims.text: The symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about God's relation to his attributes if, and only if, the instantiation relation is adopted as a constituent relation that can be modeled as parthood within a constituent ontology.

Fregean diagnostics answer the identity worry standalone, but the determinacy of divine predicates (which senses are admissible for God) is supplied only by the analogical framework, so Fregean diagnostics are insufficient for the determinacy concern without it.

The Thomistic analogical framework supplies principled admissibility constraints and a fixed metaphysical relation to creatures sufficient to exclude ill-formed divine predications, though it does not by itself determine the positive content of divine predicates such as 'good'.

Multiplicity of divine attributes must be ontologically real (differences in being, not only in sense or description), since only real multiplicity makes the attributes' non-identity a datum that simplicity must deny.

Divine simplicity implies God is identical to a property, and if that property is an abstract universal then God is an abstract object, so the personal-creator worry holds only under a Platonic theory of properties, while on trope theory it reappears as the question whether a single instantiated property can be a personal agent.
Instantiation, modeled as parthood, holds symmetrically between God and each of his attributes, so that God is part of each attribute as well as each attribute part of God.

For God and his attributes, instantiation is modeled as symmetric (mutual) parthood, so the attributes are not proper parts of God and God lacks non-symmetric parts, without commitment to fusion closure.

The truthmaker for 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' is God alone, with the contingent world-fact entering only as the content of the choice rather than as a distinct truthmaking component, and c013 and c015 are restated in terms of extrinsic content rather than extrinsic truthmakers.
If the truthmaker of God's accidental volitional property includes a contingent fact about the world, then that property is extrinsic to God, whatever its origin in God's nature.
an explicit semantic premise to block the stronger charge that conceptual multiplicity is itself a datum simplicity must deny
God is not a composite of any features on which his existence or activity depends, whether those features are ordered by priority or co-equal.
If God were composite, his unity would be grounded in distinct constituents on which his existence depends, a dependence not removed by treating those constituents as modes of a single act.

Instantiation between God and each of his attributes can be modeled as mutual parthood, which is formally consistent with God lacking non-symmetric parts, and this model is adopted as a formal option rather than as the metaphysically preferred account.

The Thomistic analogical framework excludes ill-formed divine predications only conditional on a prior, independent classification of which creaturely features are pure perfections, and it does not by itself settle contested cases such as 'God is mutable.'

If God were composite, his unity would be grounded in distinct constituents (the properties he exemplifies) on which his existence depends, whether efficiently or in grounding, so that a necessary existent that is not simple depends on what it is not.

If the truthmaker of God's accidental volitional property includes a contingent world-fact only as the content of the volition, then that property is extrinsic to God in the sense that its content depends on something contingent, while its realizer remains wholly divine.

arguments.title: Non-indexical Omniscience Fails Responsibility

atoms.A: an agent is robustly responsible for bringing about φ rather than ψ (robust contrastive responsibility obtains)
atoms.B: the agent's cognitive state represents φ as the outcome of its own action rather than ψ
atoms.C: explanations identify the agent as the source of one outcome rather than relevant alternatives
atoms.D: rationalising explanations fixing the agent as responsible source require irreducibly de se content
atoms.E: third-personal identification alone is insufficient for fixing the agent as responsible source
atoms.F: divine omniscience is strong non-indexical (strictly non-indexical, excluding irreducibly de se content)
atoms.G: strong non-indexical omniscience faces the difficulty of explaining the explanatory asymmetry between actualised and possible worlds without irreducible self-locating content
atoms.H: divine omniscience must support libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility

arguments.missing_premise: If divine omniscience must support libertarian agency and robust contrastive responsibility, then rationalising explanations that identify the agent as responsible source require irreducibly de se content. [(H -> D)]

arguments.title: Foundational Role of Worship‑Worthiness
arguments.skeleton: A -> B; ~C; A; E -> F; G -> H |- H

atoms.A: Worship is central to religious life (and to many religious traditions)
atoms.B: Questions of worship-worthiness cannot remain philosophically secondary
atoms.C: Worship has received sustained philosophical attention
atoms.D: Worship-worthiness is a question the author treats as foundational (unused placeholder)
atoms.E: Our intellectual and practical resources are finite
atoms.F: We cannot pursue every philosophical question with equal urgency
atoms.G: Worship-worthiness makes a greater axiological difference than other questions
atoms.H: Worship-worthiness (WWT) should be treated as foundational, prior to other questions in philosophy of religion

arguments.missing_premise: Worship-worthiness makes a greater axiological difference than other philosophical questions. [G]

arguments.title: No Advantage for P1 over P1*
arguments.skeleton: A & B; B & ~A; C -> E; ~F; G |- H & ~D

atoms.A: The symmetry problem for the modal ontological argument is solved or disappears in logics weaker than S5 (FLS's dialectical conclusion)
atoms.B: P1, P2, and P2* are jointly consistent in logics weaker than S5 (FLS's formal result)
atoms.C: FLS's advantage for atheists in S4 holds
atoms.D: The reverse argument (with P1*) gains a decisive advantage over the original
atoms.E: Priority is given to (P1) over its mirror (P1*)
atoms.F: The main metaphysical frameworks relevant to (P1) give it a stable advantage over (P1*)
atoms.G: Depending on their details, the frameworks support both principles, support neither, or create an asymmetry not favoring (P1)
atoms.H: Symmetry reappears at the level of necessity claims

arguments.title: Priority of Worship‑Worthiness Theology
arguments.skeleton: A; B; C & D; E |- F & G & H

atoms.A: We must first ask what is worthy of worship before asking whether God exists or what properties God has
atoms.B: Worship-worthiness theory (WWT) has priority over NWWT in several respects
atoms.C: WWT makes a greater axiological difference
atoms.D: We should focus on WWT before other theological questions
atoms.E: We should adopt WWT as the starting point, asking what is worthy of worship before any other theological question
atoms.F: WWT has axiological priority over NWWT
atoms.G: WWT has prudential priority over NWWT
atoms.H: WWT has methodological priority over NWWT

arguments.missing_premise: Each stated ground establishes its matching kind of priority: if WWT makes a greater axiological difference, it has axiological priority over NWWT; if we should focus on WWT before other questions, it has prudential priority; and if we should adopt WWT as the starting point, it has methodological priority. [(C -> F) & (D -> G) & (E -> H)]

atoms.A: God is a necessary being (on Anselmian theism)
atoms.B: Anselmian theism and genuine modal realism are jointly consistent
atoms.D: God's necessity is analysed via counterpart theory
atoms.F: A plurality of God-like individuals obtains
atoms.H: Possible worlds are maximal mereological sums of spatiotemporally connected individuals (genuine modal realism)

arguments.title: God cannot be a composite

atoms.A: God is a composite of more basic features
atoms.D: God is causally dependent on his distinct properties
atoms.E: God depends on properties such as power, wisdom, and blessedness as final causes
atoms.F: God is simple (not a composite of more basic features)

arguments.missing_premise: God is not causally dependent on his distinct properties, either efficiently or as final causes. [~D & ~E]

arguments.title: Simplicity conflicts with divine omniscience

atoms.A: God knows things other than himself
atoms.C: Knowledge of oneself is distinct from knowledge of another
atoms.D: God knows that he is causing
atoms.E: There is multiplicity in divine knowledge

arguments.title: TWI Preserves Uniqueness in GMR

atoms.A: God is unsurpassable and unmatchable (the stronger uniqueness claim)
atoms.C: TWI permits one God to create and sustain all reality
atoms.D: Those creating and sustaining abilities are required for maximal greatness
atoms.E: AT-GMRists have reason to accept TWI as the correct analysis of God's necessity
atoms.G: Using TWI inevitably produces modal collapse
atoms.H: GMR can explain God's necessary existence while preserving His uniqueness by using TWI rather than CT

arguments.missing_premise: TWI permits one God to create and sustain all reality, those abilities are required for maximal greatness, and AT-GMRists' acceptance of TWI secures GMR's explanation of necessary existence together with uniqueness. [((C & D) & (E -> H))]

arguments.title: Analogy grounds determinate theological language
arguments.skeleton: A; B; C; D; E |- F

atoms.A: The author employs Fregean distinctions from modern analytic philosophy to show how criticisms of divine simplicity can be defused
atoms.B: Fregean diagnostics must be located within the broader semantic-metaphysical framework of the doctrine of analogy
atoms.C: The analogical framework's res significata / modus significandi distinction provides the resources to ground the meaning of theological predicates
atoms.D: Analogical semantics supplies principled constraints that allow 'God is good' while excluding 'God is evil' or 'God is a chair'
atoms.E: The Thomistic doctrine of analogy provides principled constraints and sufficiently determinate content for divine predicates, answering residual worries about meaning
atoms.F: The Thomistic doctrine of analogy does not eliminate semantic openness but makes theological language sufficiently determinate for meaning and practice, grounding meaningful God-talk in metaphysics and religious practice

arguments.missing_premise: If the Thomistic doctrine of analogy supplies sufficiently determinate content and principled constraints for divine predicates, then theological language is determinate enough for meaning and practice while semantic openness is left intact, so the determinacy it supplies is what answers the worries about meaning. [E -> F]

arguments.title: Symmetry formulation viable distinct DDS

atoms.A: God lacks proper parts (DDS, mereological formulation)
atoms.B: God is identical with all his parts (DDS, identity formulation)
atoms.C: On some plausible mereological theory, something lacks proper parts by being a part of all its parts
atoms.D: Proper parthood is defined as non-symmetric parthood
atoms.E: God lacks non-symmetric parts (symmetry formulation of DDS)
atoms.G: Instantiation can plausibly be modeled as parthood
atoms.H: The symmetry formulation is viable and distinct

arguments.missing_premise: Instantiation can plausibly be modeled as parthood, so the viability premise's antecedent holds. [G]

arguments.title: Conundrum A is semantic confusion

atoms.A: Conundrum A is a semantic confusion
atoms.B: The conundrums can be diagnosed as semantic misreadings using Frege's object/concept distinction
atoms.C: Frege distinguishes the 'is' of predication from the 'is' of identification
atoms.D: In 'God is good', 'good' is a concept predicated of God, not a thing
atoms.E: Conundrum A treats 'God is good' as equivalent to 'goodness is God', mixing object-object with object-concept predication
atoms.F: Conundrum A reads the 'is' in 'God is good' as an identity 'is'

arguments.missing_premise: Given the Fregean distinctions in the premises, the diagnosis applies to Conundrum A: a conundrum that treats 'God is good' as an identity statement, equating it with 'goodness is God', is thereby a semantic confusion of exactly that kind. [(B & C & D) -> (A & E)]

arguments.title: Symmetry retains motivations and solves objections
arguments.skeleton: A & B; C; D; E |- C & D

atoms.A: The symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about God's relation to his attributes
atoms.B: Instantiation can plausibly be modeled as parthood
atoms.C: The symmetry formulation retains the usual motivations for divine simplicity (aseity, transcendence, immutability, unity)
atoms.D: The symmetry formulation addresses common objections to divine simplicity (distinctness of attributes, modal collapse)
atoms.E: The symmetry formulation allows God and his attributes to be numerically distinct, avoiding the claim that God is a property or that his attributes are identical

atoms.C: All divine attributes are identical with each other
atoms.D: There is only one divine attribute
atoms.H: The doctrine of divine simplicity is rejected

arguments.missing_premise: If divine simplicity is false, it must be rejected. [~A -> H]

atoms.C: The scopes of divine power and divine knowledge are identical

arguments.title: Extrinsic volition and knowledge solve modal collapse
arguments.skeleton: H; A -> B; C -> D; F; G |- E

atoms.B: Every non-tautological truth about God has only God as its minimal truthmaker
atoms.C: Some correct attribution to God of an accidental property has a contingent truthmaker besides God
atoms.D: Some accidental property attributed to God is at least partially extrinsic
atoms.E: A satisfactory solution to the modal collapse argument requires a theory on which volition and knowledge are extrinsic (properties a and b)
atoms.F: The truth of 'God freely chooses to create the actual world' depends on a necessary fact about God and a contingent fact about the world
atoms.G: God's relation to the world is grounded partly in facts extrinsic to God, not in contingent intrinsic facts
atoms.H: The modal collapse argument is probably the most difficult objection to divine simplicity

arguments.missing_premise: If God's relation to the world is partially based on facts extrinsic to God, then the accidental properties at issue, volition and knowledge, must be extrinsic. [G -> E]
